true_positives.matched_candidate:
All-day block comparison never matches

The unavailable-all-day branch compares two Dayjs instances with ===. That checks object identity, not time, so dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...) is always false. A date override stored with equal start and end (the usual all-day unavailable marker) never takes this path and depends on the other window checks, which do not treat a zero-length range as blocking the whole day.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override window check rejects valid slots and accepts partial overlaps

checkIfIsAvailable treats a slot as outside the date override if it is outside any one override range on that calendar day. dateOverrides.find returns the first range for which the slot ends before the range start or starts after the range end, and the caller then returns false. With two ranges on the same day (for example 09:00-11:00 and 14:00-16:00), a slot fully inside the first range is still rejected because it is outside the second. The inverse is also wrong: a slot that only partially overlaps a range does not hit either outside-condition, so it is treated as inside. Fixed-host round-robin days with more than one override, or slots that stick out of the override, are therefore bookable or hidden incorrectly.

New test does not cover fixed-host overrides or a real timezone shift

The added getSchedule call asks for Asia/Dhaka but expects the same UTC slot list already asserted for Asia/Kolkata, and it uses a personal event with no hosts. It cannot fail if fixed-host date overrides are ignored in round-robin, if an override day still ignores busy time, or if the offset math moves slots across a date boundary. The PR's stated fixes (#8207 / fixed hosts, timezone-adjusted overrides) ship with no assertion that would catch the checkIfIsAvailable regressions.

Override match returns available before busy times are checked

If any date override exists on the slot's calendar day and the slot was not rejected by the window checks, checkIfIsAvailable returns true immediately. Busy calendar events, existing bookings, and buffers passed in busy are never consulted. A fixed host who set a date override can therefore be booked on top of a meeting that falls inside that override, which is a double-booking.

Override offset is reduced to clock time and can drop the range

After shifting the override by inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset, only .hour() and .minute() are kept. A shift across midnight is applied as minutes-on-the-same-invitee-day that passed the activeOverrides filter, so the window lands on the wrong clock time (and often the wrong date). If the end crosses midnight and the start does not, endTime becomes less than startTime and buildSlots skips the range with start >= end, so that date override disappears entirely for attendees in a timezone on the other side of midnight from the organizer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing sender metadata crashes re-link

The new comparison reads integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] with no guard. build_integration only stores sender when pipeline state already has it, and older or webhook-incomplete Integration rows can be ACTIVE with zero OrganizationIntegrations — exactly the branch that reaches this line. A missing or non-dict sender raises KeyError instead of the installation-failed page, so a legitimate re-link 500s and cannot be completed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
Installation-not-found test no longer hits that path

test_installation_not_found stubs a 404 from /app/installations/{id} but then calls setup with state ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, which is not the pipeline signature (9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3). OAuthLoginView rejects the state and returns "Invalid installation request." before build_integration or the 404 handler runs. The assertion matches that generic error, so a regression in the installation-not-found path would still pass, and the old "The GitHub installation could not be found." contract is no longer covered.

Installer identity is not checked on first link

The new GitHub-user check never runs when no Integration row exists yet. OAuthLoginView records github_authenticated_user, but GitHubInstallation catches Integration.DoesNotExist and calls pipeline.next_step(), which creates the integration and organization link from the caller-supplied installation_id with no comparison to metadata sender. GitHub installation ids are enumerable and the installation webhook can arrive after this request, so an attacker who finishes any OAuth login can win that race and attach someone else's app installation to their Sentry org. Once that OrganizationIntegration exists, the later "already installed" branch blocks the real installer. The mismatch check has to fail closed until the webhook sender is known, including on this create path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
queued timestamp is frozen at import time

AssignmentSource.queued uses a bare default of timezone.now(), which Python evaluates once when the class is defined, not on each instance. Every source built via from_integration() therefore shares the same import-time timestamp, and to_dict() persists that stale value into the Celery payload. Use field(default_factory=timezone.now) if queued is meant to record when the assignment was enqueued; as written the field cannot distinguish rapid successive assignee changes.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource dict is not safe to round-trip through Celery

sync_group_assignee_outbound passes assignment_source.to_dict() straight into sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async. asdict() includes queued as a datetime. A JSON task serializer either raises TypeError (so the outbound task is never enqueued, and other linked integrations never get the assignee update) or stringifies the datetime. from_dict() then does cls(**input_dict) and only recovers a source if construction does not throw; it never parses an ISO timestamp back into a datetime, and any TypeError/ValueError returns None. The worker then calls should_sync with no source and the originating integration is not skipped, so the sync cycle this PR is meant to stop still happens after a real queue hop. The new tests run under self.tasks() eager execution, which passes the dict in-process and does not catch this.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
Cycle guard drops sync to every issue on the source integration

should_sync returns False for the whole installation when sync_source.integration_id matches org_integration.integration_id. Outbound fan-out is per ExternalIssue, but the guard has no external-issue key, so an inbound assignee change on one linked ticket suppresses outbound assignee sync for every other ticket on that same integration. A group linked to two Jira issues will leave the sibling ticket stale. It also still echoes the change to every other issue-sync integration, so two integrations with both inbound and outbound assignee sync enabled can ping-pong the assignee between themselves.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler cannot be instantiated

MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler and implements none of its abstract methods (counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, build_occurrence_and_event_data). Instantiating an ABC with unimplemented abstracts raises TypeError. Detector.detector_handler does exactly that via group_type.detector_handler(self), and MetricAlertFire still sets detector_handler to this class. Previously this handler was concrete and evaluate() returned []. Any detector whose type resolves to metric_alert_fire will now crash when processed instead of no-opping.

true_positives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
evaluate() docstring still says it returns a list

StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate now returns dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult], and process_detectors depends on .values(). The docstring still says it returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult. Callers following the docstring will iterate the dict keys (group keys) instead of the results and mishandle evaluation output.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

false_positives.candidate:
Group-key evaluation test expects the wrong occurrence

TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe builds the expected IssueOccurrence with group_key "val1" and value 6, then calls evaluate_group_key_value with group_key "group_key" and value 10. build_occurrence_and_event_data uses that group_key in the fingerprint, so the occurrence the handler returns cannot equal the expected one (fingerprint "{detector_id}:val1" vs "{detector_id}:group_key"). This assertion fails, or if equality ignores fingerprint it does not actually check the occurrence the new hook produced.

true_positives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Monitor context drops schedule_type display conversion

get_monitor_environment_context copies monitor.config and, when schedule_type is present, replaces it with get_schedule_type_display() on that copy. The returned context ignores the copy and sends monitor_environment.monitor.config instead. Occurrence events therefore keep the raw schedule_type (typically an integer enum) rather than the display string, and the conversion is dead code. Anything reading the monitor context (issue UI, consumers of the Kafka occurrence) will see the wrong schedule type.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

false_positives.candidate:
Failure-reason text does not match intended wording

get_failure_reason builds each clause as "%(count)d %(status)s" (for example "2 missed") and then appends a single "check-ins detected". For more than one status that yields strings like "2 missed, 1 timeout and 1 error check-ins detected", not the documented "2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in and 1 error check-in were detected". That string is stored as the important "Failure reason" evidence on the incident occurrence, so users see grammatically wrong, ambiguous failure summaries whenever the threshold window mixes statuses or the count is not the singular special case.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Flusher metric tags are a joined shard list

Produce/wait timers tag metrics with shard_tag = ",".join(all shards owned by that process). --flusher-processes defaults to 1, so the common case is one process for every assigned partition and a single tag value like "0,1,2,...,N". That value changes with every assignment, blows past typical tag-length limits (metrics get dropped), and is a different key on the wait timer ("shards") than on the produce timer ("shard"). Per-shard flusher health and latency dashboards will not work.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added flusher wait is a no-op under the sleep patch

test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op, then calls time.sleep(0.1) to let the flusher observe the drift update before join(). That call is the patched no-op, so it does not yield. join() sets stopped immediately; if the flusher thread has not yet run flush_segments with drift 9000, the segment is never produced and the assertion on messages fails intermittently. The new test does not actually cover the race it was added for.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added flusher wait is a no-op under the sleep patch

test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op, then calls time.sleep(0.1) to let the flusher observe the drift update before join(). That call is the patched no-op, so it does not yield. join() sets stopped immediately; if the flusher thread has not yet run flush_segments with drift 9000, the segment is never produced and the assertion on messages fails intermittently. The new test does not actually cover the race it was added for.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() skips terminate when the deadline is already spent

SpanFlusher.join() gives the entire timeout to next_step.join(), then breaks out of the process loop as soon as remaining_time <= 0, before process.terminate(). The previous single-process join always called terminate() after the wait, even if the deadline had passed. Arroyo shutdown/rebalance uses a finite join timeout, so after this change every flusher process is left running. Those processes are only daemonized, not stopped, and the consumer process stays alive across rebalance, so the old flushers keep calling flush_segments/produce on the same Redis shards as the replacement consumer. That yields duplicate buffered-segments and concurrent Redis expiry/delete races.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Failed messages are acked and never retried

OrderedQueueWorker.complete_offset runs in a finally block, including after result_processor raises, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit also add+completes the offset when decode, grouping, or put fails. The strategy docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing, but any exception is logged and then treated as done, with no DLQ on the uptime-results consumer. A transient DB or downstream failure is therefore committed (offset+1) and will not be redelivered, so an uptime check that failed to be handled can be dropped permanently. The new error-handling test asserts the opposite (no commit) and only sleeps 0.2s while the commit loop waits 1s, so it neither matches the code nor reliably checks it.

Kafka commits are invoked from a background thread

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls commit_function (the Arroyo commit callback, which reaches the librdkafka consumer) every second. Every other strategy in this consumer commits from the processing thread. librdkafka consumers are not thread-safe, and that callback races with poll, submit, and close/terminate on the main thread. terminate() does not even join the commit thread, so a commit can run while the consumer is shutting down. This can crash the consumer, commit a torn offset map, or lose the in-flight commit.

Queue-depth test races the workers and can flake

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts get_stats()['total_items'] > 0. Workers are already running and the processor is a no-op, so the queues can be empty before that assertion. test_different_groups_distributed likewise requires 20 hashed keys to land in all 3 buckets, which is not guaranteed. Both can fail on a quiet CI run without a product bug.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure

FixedQueuePool builds each queue.Queue() with the default maxsize (unlimited), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit always returns after put(). The class comment claims natural backpressure, but Arroyo will keep polling Kafka and enqueueing as fast as the broker allows. A single slow group blocks commits for its whole partition (offsets cannot advance past the oldest incomplete offset), while every later message on that partition is retained in memory. A hot or stuck subscription can therefore grow process memory without bound and turn the clog this PR is meant to avoid into an OOM, without ever pausing the consumer.

Strategy close kills the shared worker pool and stops commits before drain

The queue pool and its worker threads are created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and shared by every strategy from create_with_partitions. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets the commit-loop shutdown event, joins that thread, then calls FixedQueuePool.shutdown(). shutdown() sets each worker's shutdown flag before Queue.shutdown(), so a worker blocked in get() exits on ShutDown and does not drain remaining items, and a worker between iterations leaves the loop immediately. Offsets finished only during that drain are never committed because the commit thread is already stopped. On partition revoke/rebalance Arroyo closes this strategy and calls create_with_partitions again; the new strategy reuses the already-shut-down pool, so later messages are not processed for the rest of the process lifetime. join() also ignores its timeout and can block about 5s plus 5s per worker.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Warm permission cache no longer serves distinct denies

A permission-cache hit that does not contain the requested scope is treated as a miss and always calls getIdentityPermissions, which no longer reads the cache and always queries the DB (and then overwrites permCache). Previously one cached scope map answered every Check for that user and action. Now each distinct denied (namespace, user, action, name, folder) tuple hits the database until its denial entry is warm. Authorizing a page or search over many resources the user cannot access becomes a query stampede, and concurrent refreshes can also overwrite a newer permCache entry with an older snapshot.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Cached check error skips the DB permission fallback

If getCachedIdentityPermissions hits but checkPermission fails (typically buildFolderTree / folder store error while evaluating inheritance), Check returns the error immediately. It never reaches getIdentityPermissions, so a direct scope that exists only in the DB (the newly created dashboard/folder permission this change is meant to observe) is never loaded. A transient folder-store failure therefore fails the request even when the refreshed permission set would allow without walking the folder tree.

Denial cache pins false denies and skips permission refresh

Check writes a 30s denial (userPermDenialCacheKey) whenever the DB-backed check returns false, and the next Check returns that denial before consulting either the permission cache or the database. A negative result is often stale rather than authoritative: checkInheritedPermissions uses the separately cached folder tree, so a dashboard/folder under a newly created parent is denied even when the user has folders:uid:<parent> (or a permission row that was committed after the check). That false deny is then sticky for shortCacheTTL, including after the folder cache expires and after a later grant, which re-breaks the create-then-access case this PR is fixing. Denial entries are never deleted on a successful refresh.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Filtered Grafana rows are rendered without a key

The grafana branch of rules.map used to pass key={key} into GrafanaRuleLoader. GrafanaRuleListItem is now returned with no key, while the datasource and unknown branches still set one. As pages append, React will reuse the wrong row instances, so action menus, links, and pause/health state can attach to the wrong rule.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence action opens nothing in the list view

AlertRuleMenu can show Silence notifications from Prometheus-rule abilities and calls handleSilence, which only sets showSilenceDrawer. The drawer is rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. List items pass promRule and no ruler rule, so the click sets state and then renders nothing.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete is unreachable in the ruler-free list view

canDelete can be true from useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities when only a Prometheus rule is loaded, but the Delete item is still rendered only when rulerRule is defined, and onClick passes that rulerRule to handleDelete. GrafanaRuleListItem never supplies a ruler rule, and RuleActionsButtons already deletes via the identifier (showDeleteModal(identifier, groupIdentifier)), so the extra guard hides Delete for every Grafana rule in the new list. The group-loader menu test even asserts only four items and never looks for Delete despite granting AlertingRuleDelete.

Federated rules are always treated as editable

useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false (the old isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) check is gone, and RuleGroupIdentifierV2 cannot express source_tenants). Federated Mimir/GEM groups were previously immutable. Every consumer of useAlertRuleAbility / useAllAlertRuleAbilities will now offer edit, delete, pause, and duplicate on federated rules.

Pause never appears without a ruler rule

canPause is OR-ed with the Prometheus-rule ability so the list view can authorize pause without the ruler API, but the menu item is still gated on rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) and MenuItemPauseRule requires a RulerGrafanaRuleDTO. In the new list, rulerRule is undefined, so Pause is never shown even for users who can edit the rule.

Recording-rule export and pause dropped

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities sets ModifyExport, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently supported only when prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. The ruler path used rulerRuleType.grafana.rule, which includes Grafana recording rules. Recording rules in the list therefore lose export and pause/restore even when the user has folder edit permission and the rule is not provisioned.

Rule view links drop returnTo

The removed GrafanaRuleListItem built the view href with createReturnTo() so the detail page could navigate back to the current list URL (including filters). The replacement always links to /alerting/grafana/${uid}/view with no returnTo query. Opening a rule from the list no longer restores the filtered list on back navigation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Interpolating before the $__range guard splits queries that must stay whole

runSplitQuery now runs datasource.applyTemplateVariables before querySupportsSplitting. That helper refuses to split expressions that still contain [$__range], [$__range_s], or [$__range_ms], because those macros must be resolved against the original request range (the comment says backend interpolation on a split range is wrong). templateSrv.replace, which applyTemplateVariables uses, substitutes $__range* from the parent request before that check, so isQueryWithRangeVariable no longer matches and the query is day-split. Each chunk is then executed with the full-dashboard duration already baked in (for example [7d] on a 1-day window), which over-counts range aggregations and multiplies Loki load. The same substitution also happens in runShardSplitQuery before it delegates to runSplitQuery, so the shard path has the same hole.

Pre-interpolating range vars breaks stream-shard selector rewrite

runShardSplitQuery now expands variables with applyTemplateVariables before interpolateShardingSelector rewrites the stream selector (line 154). interpolateShardingSelector inserts the shard matcher and `| drop __stream_shard__` by replacing the `{...}` selector only. If a range like [$__auto] is still attached to that selector, the rewrite keeps a valid range vector; after this change [$__auto] is already `5m`, so the range is left behind the inserted pipeline. The new test locks in the result: `count_over_time({a="b", __stream_shard__=~"20|10"} | drop __stream_shard__[5m])`, which is invalid LogQL (count_over_time requires a range vector, and [5m] is bound to the drop stage). Sharded metric queries whose range or step is a variable will fail or return errors.

applyTemplateVariables runs again on already interpolated shard requests

runShardSplitQuery already maps every target through applyTemplateVariables(query, scopedVars, request.filters) and then calls runSplitQuery on each shard subrequest. runSplitQuery applies the same function again, still passing request.filters. applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent when filters are present: ad-hoc matchers are appended to expr on every call, so each sharded subquery gets duplicate label matchers and can be rejected by Loki. The updated shard test expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times (once up front plus once per group inside runSplitQuery), which confirms the re-entry, but nothing asserts that filters or escaped matchers survive a second pass.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plugin completion logs drop traceID

logRequest no longer appends traceID from tracing.TraceIDFromContext, and ContextualLoggerMiddleware only puts endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname on the context. The "Plugin Request Completed" / grafana-data-egress line therefore no longer carries a trace id, so those logs can no longer be correlated with the request trace. Put traceID back on the log params (or into the contextual attributes) before relying on FromContext.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext drops recorded logs

FromContext ignores the receiver and returns NewTestLogger(). LoggerMiddleware now logs via logger.FromContext(ctx).Info, so any test that injects a TestLogger and asserts InfoLogs will see zero calls: the Info lands on a different instance. FromContext should return the same TestLogger (or a child that still records into it).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is not atomic with the insert

CreateOrUpdateDevice reads CountDevices and, only if the count is still under deviceLimit, performs a separate INSERT. Those steps are not in one transaction and are not serialized with the existing server lock, so concurrent anonymous requests (including across Grafana replicas sharing the database) can all observe count < limit and all insert. The configured cap can be exceeded by the number of in-flight creates, and nothing in the schema enforces the limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit is bypassed after the first request

tagDeviceUI writes the device cache key before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns. When the store is at the limit, a new device's first TagDevice call fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached (so Authenticate denies that request), but the key is already cached for 29 minutes. Every later request for that device ID hits the cache and returns nil without touching the database, so anonymous authentication succeeds and the device is never counted. The configured limit therefore only fails a single attempt per device per cache TTL and does not actually cap anonymous access.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
New auth.anonymous device_limit setting is undocumented

AnonymousDeviceLimit is read from auth.anonymous device_limit (default 0, meaning unlimited), but this change does not add the key to defaults.ini / sample.ini or any docs. Operators have no documented way to discover the setting, its default, or that 0 disables enforcement, so the feature cannot be configured as intended.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Leftover Error logs dump every cleanup batch, including all IDs

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log successful fetch/delete steps with log.Error, including the full ID slice and SQL condition (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579). These fire on every batch, even when nothing is deleted. In production that spams error-level logs and can serialize tens of thousands of IDs per batch (the new test uses a batch size of 32767), adding load and drowning real errors. These should be removed or dropped to debug without the ID list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job interval accidentally reduced from 10 minutes to 1

Run() now starts the cleanup ticker at 1 minute instead of 10. Nothing in this change describes or tests a schedule change, and clean() still uses a 9-minute timeout, so this looks like leftover debug. After merge, annotation cleanup (and every other cleanup job) runs about 10x more often, increasing DB load and lock contention—the opposite of the deadlock fix—and a slow run can still be in progress when the next tick is due.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Storage failures and legacy delete-collection are recorded on the wrong histogram

Create and Update record a storage error with recordLegacyDuration (lines 45 and 129), so a unified-storage failure is counted as a legacy-storage failure and is missing from the storage histogram. DeleteCollection's async legacy call (line 166) uses recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency and errors are attributed to unified storage. Mode 3 latency/error dashboards will be wrong and can hide a broken legacy backfill.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful Delete records the object name as the metric kind label

On the Delete success path, recordStorageDuration is called with name (the object name) where every other call passes options.Kind. If that argument is a Prometheus label, each deleted object creates a new series and cardinality grows without bound. The error path on the previous line correctly uses options.Kind, so success and failure are also not comparable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled on return

Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s). That child is still cancelled as soon as the incoming request context is cancelled, which happens when the handler returns the unified-storage result. The 10s timeout never applies. The legacy "safe measure" write is therefore raced against request completion and will usually fail with context.Canceled, so legacy storage diverges from unified storage with no retry. Derive the background work from context.WithoutCancel (then apply the timeout), and log the legacy error instead of only recording a metric.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy goroutines

Destroy closes Storage and Legacy immediately while Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection may still be running legacy writes in detached goroutines. Those calls can hit a destroyed backend (panic or lost write) during shutdown or mode switch, and there is no way for the caller to know the backfill finished.

Legacy Update reuses the same UpdatedObjectInfo concurrently

After Storage.Update returns, the goroutine calls Legacy.Update with the same objInfo value. UpdatedObjectInfo implementations typically cache the computed object or mutate internal state on the first UpdatedObject call, and Storage.Update may still be using that state. Running both updates at once races on that shared object and no longer writes the unified-storage result into legacy (the previous code snapshotted the updated object and applied that exact object to legacy). Legacy can fail optimistic concurrency, apply a different patch, or panic, so the two stores diverge.

Mode 3 tests never observe the async legacy write and mock the wrong store on errors

The Create error case is named as a unified-storage failure but only stubs Legacy.Create, and Storage.Create has no expectation, so the test does not exercise the path it claims. Success cases start legacy work in a goroutine and return without AssertCalled, a wait, or AssertExpectations, so a missing or panicked legacy write still passes. The playlist mode 3 integration test then reads the legacy API immediately after a k8s write, which will flake or fail for the same unsynchronized async path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write path never rechecks cache and can wipe a good value

GetWebAssets drops the read lock, then later takes the write lock and always reloads and assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result (line 69), including when the load fails and result is nil. There is no second check of entryPointAssetsCache under the write lock. Two callers can both observe a nil cache; the first populates it successfully and the second then overwrites that pointer with nil (or a redundant load) if its file read fails. Later non-dev requests miss the cache and fail until a later load succeeds. After Lock(), return the existing cache when Env is not Dev and it is already non-nil, and do not store a nil/error result over a successful one.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write path never rechecks cache and can wipe a good value

GetWebAssets drops the read lock, then later takes the write lock and always reloads and assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result (line 69), including when the load fails and result is nil. There is no second check of entryPointAssetsCache under the write lock. Two callers can both observe a nil cache; the first populates it successfully and the second then overwrites that pointer with nil (or a redundant load) if its file read fails. Later non-dev requests miss the cache and fail until a later load succeeds. After Lock(), return the existing cache when Env is not Dev and it is already non-nil, and do not store a nil/error result over a successful one.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL disable is a dead flag check that always returns false

enableSqlExpressions reads FlagSqlExpressions, inverts it, and then returns false from both branches. SQL expressions are therefore always rejected, but the check does not implement a real allow/deny policy and looks like a mistaken edit. A later cleanup that “fixes” the inversion (return the flag, or return true when the flag is on) would re-open the DuckDB SQL expression path that this change is meant to kill for CVE-2024-9264. The disable should be an obvious unconditional false (or the SQL command type removed), not a flag read whose result is discarded.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test that SQL expressions cannot run

The security fix only stubs sql.DB and adds a gate in ExpressionQueryReader. UnmarshalSQLCommand still builds a SQLCommand and Execute still calls QueryFramesInto; both fail only because the new stubs return "not implemented". Nothing in this change asserts that a SQL expression query is rejected on the reader path and on UnmarshalSQLCommand/Execute, or that no DuckDB/process call is made. A partial revert that restores a real TablesList or QueryFramesInto would ship without a failing test.

Rejection error says SQL expressions are unimplemented

When a SQL expression is parsed, ReadQuery returns fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented"). That text is wrong: the type was implemented and is being hard-disabled because DuckDB evaluation allowed RCE/LFI. Operators and the still-documented feature flag will treat this as a missing feature to turn back on, not as an intentional security shutdown. The error should say SQL expressions are disabled.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex no longer serializes builds of the same key

BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the whole build, which also prevented two callers from indexing the same NamespacedResource at once. The lock is now taken only to insert the finished index. getOrCreateIndex is still check-then-act (GetIndex nil, then build), and init runs builds with an errgroup, so two builds of one key can overlap. The later insert overwrites the cache: the discarded index may already have watch updates applied, and the winner is a stale snapshot, so search silently misses writes. For file indexes, a second bleve.New on the same directory can also fail or corrupt the on-disk index. Per-key singleflight (or a lock held from the nil check through cache insert) is required; a shorter global lock alone does not fix the lost-update window.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs ranges the index cache without cacheMu

TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no lock. search.init now starts the watch goroutine and then immediately calls TotalDocs for the new startup log. That goroutine can handle a write for a namespace that was not prebuilt and call BuildIndex, which writes b.cache under cacheMu. Concurrent map iteration and write panics the process during startup. TotalDocs must take cacheMu.RLock (and BuildIndex must keep the write lock around the map update).

false_positives.candidate:
Index init goroutines race on shared err and counter

The errgroup workers in init all assign the outer err from build() and increment totalBatchesIndexed with no synchronization. With WorkerThreads > 1 (the concurrency this change is trying to use), that is a data race: a worker can return another worker's nil and hide a failed namespace build, so Init succeeds while that index was never built. The span attribute namespaced_indexed is also racy. Each worker needs its own error variable, and the counter needs atomic increment or a post-Wait tally.

Startup watch starts at latest RV and drops events written during index build

init lists each namespace via build(), which returns the resource version observed by that list, then ignores it. Only after every namespace has been indexed does it call WatchWriteEvents, which records listLatestRVs at that later moment and polls strictly after those versions. Any write committed after a namespace's list snapshot and before the watch baseline (other storage-server replicas, or the main Grafana process writing the same DB while this process is still starting) is neither in the built index nor replayed. Moving this work into NewResourceServer makes that window the entire startup index build. The watch must resume from the RV returned by each build, not from the RV at the end of all builds.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Login-cache test cleanup deletes the wrong IdP alias

testCacheIDPForLogin registers cleanup with testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove (also at the hide-on-login provider created later in the same test). The providers are actually created as idp-alias-0 through idp-alias-20, so cleanup issues DELETE for a non-existent alias "alias" and leaves every created broker in the shared test realm. Later tests that count identity providers, including testCacheIDPByOrg's expectation of 6 providers for an organization, can fail or become order-dependent, and the new test does not isolate its data.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation uses wrapped isEnabled and skips real membership changes

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate treats the pre-update model from getById as the source of truth for whether the IdP is a login IdP. With the organization feature on, getById returns a wrapper whose isEnabled() is false whenever the linked organization is missing, disabled, or the organization provider is disabled, even if the stored IdP is enabled. LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate uses that isEnabled(). The getForLogin cache, however, is filled from the JPA query, which only checks the IdP's own enabled, link-only, hide-on-login, and broker-public flags. If the org is disabled (so the wrapped original already fails the predicate) and the update also fails the predicate — for example hide-on-login or link-only is set, broker-public is cleared, or the IdP enabled flag is turned off — both sides fail and the method returns without invalidating the login list caches. Those lists still contain the IdP. After the organization is enabled again, getById shows the updated flags, but OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled(), not hide-on-login or link-only, so a hidden or link-only broker can be offered on the login page until the cache expires.

getForLogin cache drops result order

Cached login results are stored in a Set of internal ids and returned from a HashSet. The previous getForLogin implementation returned the delegate stream order (stable storage order, typically alias or guiOrder). HashSet iteration order is undefined and can change between calls even when the membership is unchanged. Callers that do not sort, unlike OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean, will show identity-provider buttons in a shuffling order.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider

getBouncyCastleProvider is documented and used as the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) JCA provider. This implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the JDK keystore provider (typically SUN), not BouncyCastle. WildFlyElytronProvider correctly returns null when BC is absent. When this provider is the one CryptoIntegration selects, callers that register or use getBouncyCastleProvider() will treat a non-BC provider as BouncyCastle and either register the wrong provider or invoke BC-only algorithms against it and fail. Return null if no BC provider is available.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementors

order() was added as an abstract method on the public CryptoProvider SPI with no default. Any out-of-tree or not-yet-updated CryptoProvider implementation no longer compiles or loads. A default such as order() returning 0 would keep old providers working and still let the in-tree providers (200) and AuthzClientCryptoProvider (100) win via the new sort.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
ECDSA tests use one P-256 key and only check a symmetric round trip

The suite generates a single KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") key (platform default, P-256) and reuses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512. R and S are therefore always ~32-byte P-256 integers, then padded to 48 or 66 bytes. The only assertion is that asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(rs)) equals rs. A conversion that drops high bytes, mishandles the DER sign byte, or emits unverifiable ASN.1 still passes, and ES384/ES512 are never exercised at their real coordinate sizes. Generate a key on the matching curve (P-256/P-384/P-521) and check Signature.verify on the DER form produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER.

Equal-order crypto providers are no longer rejected

detectProvider used to fail startup when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. It now sorts by order() descending and silently keeps the first winner, logging the rest only at debug. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so a deployment that accidentally has two of those modules (the case the old check existed for) now boots with whichever ServiceLoader returns first. A FIPS provider can be ignored in favor of the non-FIPS default, or the reverse, with no error. Tie on order should still be a hard failure; only a strictly lower order (the new authz-client provider at 100) should be ignored.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Per-client resources are created without a type

getOrCreateResource creates the client resource with resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner) and only updateScopes. It never sets the resource type to CLIENTS, unlike init() which calls resource.setType(type) for the all-clients resource. ClientPermissionsV2.getClientsWithPermission lists candidates with resourceStore.findByType(..., CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE). Per-client grants are therefore omitted from that set, so admin list/filter paths that rely on getClientsWithPermission drop clients the caller is actually allowed to see. The same query can also include the all-clients resource whose name is the literal "Clients", which is not a client id.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing all-clients resource causes NPE

hasPermission(ClientModel, String) falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource when no per-client resource exists, then immediately calls PolicyStore.findByResource(server, resource) and later evaluatePermission without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when the "Clients" resource was never created (see init() early return on an existing admin-permissions client). A view/manage/configure check then throws NullPointerException instead of returning false, so admin API calls 500 rather than 403.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Client resource names are not resolved

getResourceName only special-cases the Users resource type. Client resources are stored under the internal client id and typically have a null display name, so the method returns null (or a blank display name) for Clients policies. Admin permission APIs and the console therefore show an empty resource name instead of the clientId for client-scoped permissions.

Existing admin-permissions client is not migrated

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set and never adds the new Clients resource type or the configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite scopes. Realms that initialized FGAP V2 when only Users existed keep the old resource server. Creating or evaluating a Clients permission then fails in getScope with "Scope [configure] does not exist" (or the equivalent for the other new scopes), so the feature does not work after upgrade.

Map-role checks ignore manage-clients admins

canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission and never root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS) or canManage(client). When ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is on, MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() always returns this class, so realm admins who only have the manage-clients role are denied mapping client roles, composite roles, and client-scope roles unless a separate FGAP policy exists. Those operations 403 for users who are allowed to manage the client.

V2 client permission methods throw instead of denying

canExchangeTo, isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, and the permission-policy accessors throw UnsupportedOperationException. With the V2 feature enabled, every clients() call uses this class. Token-exchange checks and the client management-permissions admin endpoints therefore 500 instead of returning false or a disabled permissions representation. The removal listener was gated to the V1 feature, but these other callers were not.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Default update-strategy tests never enable rolling-updates

createInitialDeployment returns immediately when updateStrategy is null, and the new spec.features.enabled: rolling-updates assignment is only reached for an explicit strategy. The parameterized cases include null, which is the default "mimic 26.1" path: testImageChange(null) and testCacheMaxCount(null) deploy a CR without the feature. The operator guide added in this PR says the operator fails unless rolling-updates is enabled, and those tests still assert recreate/rolling status. As written, the default-strategy cases either fail reconciliation or only pass because some other image build happens to bake the feature in, so they do not actually cover the configuration users are told to use.

Exit-code contract is not asserted

This change makes exit status the public contract: recreate incompatibility moves from 4 to 3, and a disabled rolling-updates feature must exit 4. testFeatureNotEnabled only checks the error string, and testWrongVersions only checks the incompatibility message. Neither asserts result.exitCode(). That gap already hid the previous mismatch (code returned 4 while the guide documented 3), so a regression of 0/3/4 will still leave CI green and break scripts that branch on the exit code.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Group canManage() treats VIEW as manage

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns true when hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE) succeeds, so a caller who only has the Groups VIEW scope is treated as allowed to manage every group. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() (and any other requireManage() caller) therefore lets a view-only fine-grained admin create groups. V1 canManage() only checks MANAGE_USERS, and canManage(GroupModel) correctly checks only MANAGE. The VIEW scope must not satisfy canManage(); the interface comment that lists VIEW looks copied from canView().

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
View-members group filter uses authz resource ids

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() walks resources with findByType and then calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) and granted.add(groupResource.getId()). V2 group resources are stored under the group id as the resource name (resolveGroup returns group.getId()), while getId() is the authorization resource UUID. hasPermission looks that value up with findByName, so the per-group permission check misses and falls back to the all-groups resource. The set passed to UserModel.GROUPS / getUsersCount is therefore not a set of group ids. User search and user counts for admins who can only view members of specific groups (UsersResource, BruteForceUsersResource) will drop those users or match the wrong groups.

false_positives.candidate:
Created group resources never get type Groups

getOrCreateResource() creates a resource and updates scopes but never calls resource.setType(resourceType). V1 group resources were typed "Group". GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() only discovers groups via resourceStore.findByType(..., GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE). Without the type, individual group permission resources are invisible to that scan, so membership-based user visibility cannot be computed even after the id/name mix-up is fixed. The all-groups resource created in init() does set the type; per-object resources must do the same.

Existing admin-permissions clients are not upgraded for Groups

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already non-null, and that is the only place scopes and the "Groups" resource type are created. Realms that already enabled FGAP V2 (client created with only Users/Clients) never receive GROUPS, manage-membership, manage-members, or view-members. Creating a group permission then fails in getOrCreateResource with ModelException "No scopes found", and GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission() NPEs when getResourceTypeResource() returns null and that null is passed to policyStore.findByResource / resource.getScopes(). Schema init needs an idempotent update path for new resource types and scopes.

requireManageMembers javadoc cites the wrong check

The javadoc on requireManageMembers says it throws if canManageMembership(GroupModel) is false. The implementation throws when canManageMembers is false. Callers reading only the interface will enforce or test the wrong scope (manage-membership vs manage-members).

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian login string replaced with Italian

loginTotpStep1 in the Lithuanian login bundle was replaced with 'Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:' which is Italian, not Lithuanian. Users with locale lt will see an Italian TOTP setup instruction.

true_positives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Simplified Chinese account string written in Traditional Chinese

totpStep1 in messages_zh_CN.properties was replaced with '在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一：', which uses Traditional characters (手機, 應用程式, 安裝). The rest of this zh_CN file is Simplified Chinese. zh_CN users will see a Traditional Chinese TOTP instruction.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
Account UI message switched to Java MessageFormat placeholders

error-invalid-multivalued-size was changed from i18next placeholders ({{0}}, {{1}}, {{2}}) to Java MessageFormat ({0} and a {2,choice,...} pattern). Every other string in this account-ui bundle still uses {{0}}-style interpolation. The account UI will not substitute the attribute name or limits, and users will see the raw choice-format pattern, including the '<' selector, instead of a readable validation error.

Admin UI message switched to Java MessageFormat placeholders

error-invalid-multivalued-size in the React admin console bundle was changed from {{0}}/{{1}}/{{2}} to a Java MessageFormat choice pattern. This bundle is not formatted with java.text.MessageFormat; the admin UI will show the literal '{0}' and '{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}' text instead of the attribute name and value counts.

Diff highlighter throws when prefix and suffix overlap

When sanitized and original differ, the report trims a shared prefix and suffix and then calls substring(start, length - end) with no check that start <= length - end. If the common prefix and suffix overlap (for example original 'aaa' vs sanitized 'aa'), length - end is less than start and String.substring throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. verify() does not catch RuntimeException, so one illegal message aborts the whole theme-verifier run instead of reporting the violation.

Lithuanian account string replaced with Italian

totpStep1 in the Lithuanian account bundle was replaced with the same Italian sentence ('Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:'). The previous Lithuanian text was removed, so the account theme shows the wrong language for this step.

Message bundles are decoded as ISO-8859-1

verifySafeHtml loads files with PropertyResourceBundle(InputStream), which always decodes as ISO-8859-1. Keycloak theme message files are UTF-8 (the same files contain raw Chinese, Arabic, and other non-Latin text). The sanitizer therefore runs on mojibake, not the strings that are shipped, so it can fail the build on legitimate translations or miss HTML that only differs after a UTF-8 decode. Use a UTF-8 Reader (PropertyResourceBundle(Reader) or an InputStreamReader).

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

false_positives.candidate:
Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure

FixedQueuePool builds each queue.Queue() with the default maxsize (unlimited), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit always returns after put(). The class comment claims natural backpressure, but Arroyo will keep polling Kafka and enqueueing as fast as the broker allows. A single slow group blocks commits for its whole partition (offsets cannot advance past the oldest incomplete offset), while every later message on that partition is retained in memory. A hot or stuck subscription can therefore grow process memory without bound and turn the clog this PR is meant to avoid into an OOM, without ever pausing the consumer.

Strategy close kills the shared worker pool and stops commits before drain

The queue pool and its worker threads are created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and shared by every strategy from create_with_partitions. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets the commit-loop shutdown event, joins that thread, then calls FixedQueuePool.shutdown(). shutdown() sets each worker's shutdown flag before Queue.shutdown(), so a worker blocked in get() exits on ShutDown and does not drain remaining items, and a worker between iterations leaves the loop immediately. Offsets finished only during that drain are never committed because the commit thread is already stopped. On partition revoke/rebalance Arroyo closes this strategy and calls create_with_partitions again; the new strategy reuses the already-shut-down pool, so later messages are not processed for the rest of the process lifetime. join() also ignores its timeout and can block about 5s plus 5s per worker.

Kafka commits are invoked from a background thread

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls commit_function (the Arroyo commit callback, which reaches the librdkafka consumer) every second. Every other strategy in this consumer commits from the processing thread. librdkafka consumers are not thread-safe, and that callback races with poll, submit, and close/terminate on the main thread. terminate() does not even join the commit thread, so a commit can run while the consumer is shutting down. This can crash the consumer, commit a torn offset map, or lose the in-flight commit.

Failed messages are acked and never retried

OrderedQueueWorker.complete_offset runs in a finally block, including after result_processor raises, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit also add+completes the offset when decode, grouping, or put fails. The strategy docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing, but any exception is logged and then treated as done, with no DLQ on the uptime-results consumer. A transient DB or downstream failure is therefore committed (offset+1) and will not be redelivered, so an uptime check that failed to be handled can be dropped permanently. The new error-handling test asserts the opposite (no commit) and only sleeps 0.2s while the commit loop waits 1s, so it neither matches the code nor reliably checks it.

Queue-depth test races the workers and can flake

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts get_stats()['total_items'] > 0. Workers are already running and the processor is a no-op, so the queues can be empty before that assertion. test_different_groups_distributed likewise requires 20 hashed keys to land in all 3 buckets, which is not guaranteed. Both can fail on a quiet CI run without a product bug.

Keys written before deploy remain SETs until redis_ttl (default 3600s). Any Z* command against those keys returns WRONGTYPE, so process_spans and flush_segments fail for in-flight segments and those spans are dropped or stuck until TTL. A rolling deploy cannot safely mix old and new consumers on the same keys.

Running both updates at once races on that shared object and no longer writes the unified-storage result into legacy (the previous code snapshotted the updated object and applied that exact object to legacy). Legacy can fail optimistic concurrency, apply a different patch, or panic, so the two stores diverge.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy goroutines

Destroy closes Storage and Legacy immediately while Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection may still be running legacy writes in detached goroutines. Those calls can hit a destroyed backend (panic or lost write) during shutdown or mode switch, and there is no way for the caller to know the backfill finished.

Success cases start legacy work in a goroutine and return without AssertCalled, a wait, or AssertExpectations, so a missing or panicked legacy write still passes. The playlist mode 3 integration test then reads the legacy API immediately after a k8s write, which will flake or fail for the same unsynchronized async path.

Username and avatar therefore render blank, and removeMember is invoked with undefined, so the DELETE is sent without a user id (or not at all). The template should bind `username` / `this` (or `view.content`) on the item context.

remove_member deletes by raw id and skips Group#remove

`group.users.delete(user_id)` passes an Integer. On the Rails 4.1 association API this app uses, `has_many#delete` type-checks each argument and raises `ActiveRecord::AssociationTypeMismatch` unless the value is a User, so every removal 500s and the membership is unchanged (the new spec would fail). Even on a Rails version that accepts ids, `delete` skips `Group#remove` / GroupUser callbacks that the old patch path used, so counter caches and primary-group cleanup are not run. Load the user and call `group.remove(user)`.

Creating a group drops alias_level

`create` only assigns `name` and `visible`. The admin form shows the alias-level combo before the group has an id, and `Group#asJSON` / `Group#create` send `alias_level`, but the controller never reads it. A group created with "everyone" or "mods and admins" is stored at the column default (nobody) until a later update. `update` already applies `params[:alias_level]`; `create` needs the same assignment.

members offset/limit are not clamped

`offset = params[:offset].to_i` is passed straight to SQL. A negative offset (easy to send, and the client can also land past the end after the last member of a page is removed because the server echoes the requested offset) makes PostgreSQL raise `OFFSET must not be negative` and turns the members request into a 500. Limit is also unbounded, so `?limit=` can force the public members endpoint to load an entire automatic group (trust_level_0) into one response. Clamp offset to `>= 0` and to the last page, and cap limit.

Add/remove membership failures are swallowed

`removeMember` and `addMembers` only chain `.then` to reload the list. A 422 (automatic group, validation error) or network failure never surfaces a message, unlike `save`/`destroy` which bootbox the error. The admin UI keeps the old member list with no indication the change did not stick.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Block check writes stats and is counted twice per signup

should_block? increments match_count and saves last_match_at as a side effect of validation, using a non-atomic read-modify-write. UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save, and save validates again, so one signup attempt runs EmailValidator twice and advances match_count by 2. Concurrent attempts can also lose updates. last_match_at and match_count therefore do not record how many times the address was actually submitted, which breaks the statistic this table is added to track.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same core issue: the predicate method checking if an email should be blocked has the side effect of updating statistics (match_count/last_match_at) during a read/validation operation, leading to race conditions and inaccurate counts.

true_positives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

Domain allow/deny regex is unanchored

email_in_restriction_setting? builds Regexp.new("@(#{domains})") and tests it with =~, with no end anchor and with only "." escaped. A blacklist entry of "gmail.com" therefore matches "user@gmail.com.evil.test" as well as the real domain, and a whitelist entry likewise treats that host as allowed. Attackers can evade the domain blacklist (and pass a whitelist) by appending another label, so the restriction this validator is supposed to enforce does not hold.
