true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and unnormalized

BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the address with an exact BlockedEmail.where(email: email) match, and neither this method nor EmailValidator downcases or strips the value first. PostgreSQL's unique index is also case-sensitive, so a row stored as "bad@spam.com" will not match a signup of "Bad@spam.com" or " bad@spam.com". The block is therefore bypassed by trivial casing or whitespace changes, and the new blocked-email control does not actually stop the address it was meant to stop.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same vulnerability as the golden comment: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a case-sensitive lookup, allowing users to bypass the block by altering the casing of their email address.

true_positives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Header panel right alignment fails outside modern flex

.panel no longer uses float: right. Right alignment is only margin-left: auto plus order(3), and .d-header .contents is a flex container via the new mixin (including display: -webkit-box / -ms-flexbox). Auto margins do not absorb free space in the 2009 -webkit-box model those prefixes turn on, and in any browser that ignores display: flex the panel is a normal block whose auto margin computes to 0. The icons, login, and sign-up controls then stay on the left under the logo instead of the right side of the header. The prefixed mixin does not provide a float fallback for the technique that replaced float: right.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same change (the removal of `float: right` on `.d-header .panel` in favor of flexbox alignment) and the same visual symptom (the login panel stacking on the left/under the title instead of being right-aligned). Although they highlight slightly different scenarios where this breaks (the golden comment points to the non-Ember/noscript DOM structure where `.panel` is not a direct flex item, while the candidate points to older browsers/webkit-box fallbacks where `margin-left: auto` fails), they fundamentally point to the same code change and resulting layout regression.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order mixin uses one number for 0-based and 1-based flex specs

@mixin order writes the same $val to -webkit-box-ordinal-group, -ms-flex-order, and order. -webkit-box-ordinal-group is 1-based (initial value 1; 0 is invalid) while order and -ms-flex-order are 0-based (initial value 0). Call sites pass order(2) on .extra-info-wrapper and order(3) on .panel. In old WebKit those become ordinal groups 2 and 3 against siblings that stay at the default of 1, so source order among any items that should share a slot will not match modern flex, and a later order(0) or order(1) would be dropped or tied with defaults. The prefixed value needs to be $val + 1 for -webkit-box-ordinal-group.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` uses 1-based indexing (where 0 is invalid) while `order` uses 0-based indexing, so passing the same `$val` directly to both causes layout rendering bugs in older browsers.

false_positives.candidate:
Custom action message paragraphs lose vertical separation

.small-action .custom-message p margin was changed from 5px 0 to 0 as part of the flex alignment tweak. That rule is the spacing between paragraphs inside the moderator/small-action custom message, which is not a flex item and is not centered by align-items on .small-action. Multi-paragraph action descriptions now render as a single unspaced block.

Header flex items cannot shrink, so long titles push the panel off-screen

.d-header .contents is display: flex with no min-width: 0, overflow, or flex-shrink override on its children. Flex items default to min-width: auto, so they will not shrink below their content. .extra-info-wrapper (order 2, the docked topic title) and the logo title sit in that row with .panel (margin-left: auto, order 3). A long topic title therefore forces the row wider than the viewport and shoves the header icons off-screen instead of ellipsizing, which the previous float layout did not do. Set min-width: 0 and overflow/text-overflow on the title/extra-info flex items.

false_negatives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
website_name bypasses TL0 field hiding

include_website_name is never consulted: ActiveModel::Serializer only calls include_website_name?. website_name is also missing from untrusted_attributes, unlike website. Anonymous viewers of a TL0 user therefore still get website_name (host, and host+path when it matches the instance), which is the same profile URL the serializer is supposed to withhold. The new specs never cover a TL0/anonymous viewer, so this leak is untested.

false_positives.candidate:
Same-domain path display fails on case and www

Hosts are compared case-sensitively and without normalizing a leading www. A site at example.com will not treat http://Example.com/user or http://www.example.com/user as the same domain (lengths differ, and example.com does not end with .www.example.com), so the profile shows only the host. The inverse (instance on www, website on the apex) does append the path, so the feature is inconsistent with its own parent-domain rule. Comparisons should downcase both hosts and treat a single www label as equivalent before deciding whether to append the path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Resize messages accepted from any origin that is a substring of discourseUrl

The check is `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1`, not an equality check against the forum origin. Any `e.origin` that appears inside `discourseUrl` is trusted. For example `http://localhost` matches `http://localhost:3000`, and a short prefix such as `https://forum` matches `https://forum.example.com`. A page on that origin can post a `discourse-resize` message and set the iframe height.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same vulnerability: the origin validation uses `indexOf` instead of a strict origin check, allowing an attacker with a matching substring/domain to bypass the check.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin is a full referer URL

`parent.postMessage(..., '<%= request.referer %>')` passes the full referer (scheme, host, path, and query). `postMessage` requires an origin (`scheme://host[:port]`) or `*`. A path-bearing referer throws, so the parent never receives `discourse-resize` and the iframe stays at its default height.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: passing the full referrer URL as the `targetOrigin` in `postMessage` instead of just the origin (scheme+host+port), which breaks the resize functionality.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Any embed_url is enqueued after a spoofable referer check

Host allowlisting happens only later in `TopicRetriever`, not before `Jobs.enqueue`. The referer check uses a client-supplied header, so a caller can set `Referer` to the configured host and enqueue `retrieve_topic` for arbitrary `embed_url` values. That floods the job queue; URLs that do match `embeddable_host` are then fetched server-side with `open` (no timeout, redirects followed).
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same underlying vulnerability: relying on the easily spoofable HTTP Referer header for host validation. While the golden comment also mentions X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL and the candidate focuses on the downstream effect of job enqueuing, the core broken security control (spoofable referer check) is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Imported URL is interpolated into HTML unsafely The imported-from footer builds `#{url}` from the source URL after only checking that it starts with http/https. A URL containing a quote or other markup (for example `http://evil.test/' onclick='alert(1)`) breaks out of the attribute. Combined with the raw_html cook path, that markup is stored and rendered as HTML.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment identifies two issues: a potential NoMethodError on nil contents and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped URL interpolation into HTML. The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact XSS vulnerability from the unescaped URL interpolation in the anchor tag.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Embed template has invalid ERB and will not render

`<%- end if %>` is not valid ERB/Ruby (it must be `<% end %>`). Rendering `embed/best` raises a syntax error, so every successful embed that already has a topic returns 500 instead of the discussion iframe.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: using `end if` instead of `end` in an ERB template, which causes a syntax error in Ruby/ERB.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed poll crashes when an item has no content

`i.content.scrub` assumes every SimpleRSS item has an HTML `content` string. RSS 2.0 items usually only have `description`, and `content` is nil, so the hourly job raises NoMethodError and imports nothing. `CGI.unescapeHTML` on that body also turns escaped markup (`<script>`) into live tags before it is stored as raw HTML.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: calling `i.content.scrub` will crash with a NoMethodError when `i.content` is nil, which is common in RSS feeds that only provide `description`.

false_positives.candidate:
raw_html posts skip cooking and sanitization

When `cook_method` is `raw_html`, `cook` returns `raw` unchanged and never runs the normal pipeline or Sanitize. Feed and readability imports store that HTML as the post body (`TopicEmbed.import` sets this cook method and `skip_validations: true`). The embed view then emits it with `raw post.cooked`, and the forum will too. A feed item or fetched page can therefore inject script/markup that runs on the Discourse origin for anyone who views the topic or the embed.

Embed controller spec expects a retriever the action never calls

The example stubs `TopicRetriever.new` and expects `#retrieve` when no embed exists. `EmbedController#best` only calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)`. That expectation fails, so the new controller spec does not pass and does not actually cover the enqueue path, referer/host mismatch, or the loading template.

embed_url is limited to 255 characters

`t.string :embed_url` uses the default varchar(255) and a unique index. Article and feed URLs with long paths or query strings exceed that and `TopicEmbed.create!` fails, so those pages never embed and the retrieve job errors instead of importing.

Each cache miss synchronously polls the entire feed

`perform_retrieve` calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline whenever feed polling is enabled and this URL is not yet embedded. That opens the feed with no timeout and imports every item on the request/job that is only trying to fetch one URL. A slow or huge feed blocks the worker, and many distinct embed URLs repeat the full poll.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second downsize definition overwrites the width/height API

Ruby does not overload methods. The new downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts) at this line replaces the downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts) defined just above, so that width/height implementation is dead. Existing callers that pass numeric max width and height now treat the width as a geometry string and the height integer as opts. optimize then evaluates opts[:allow_animation] and raises NoMethodError, so thumbnail downsizing that still uses the old signature breaks.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the `downsize` method is defined twice, causing the second definition (taking `dimensions`) to overwrite the first definition (taking `max_width` and `max_height`), which makes the original method unreachable and breaks callers using the old signature.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upload size cap hardcoded to 10MB for every type

validateUploadedFile used to enforce Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so images and attachments had separate admin-configured limits. It now always uses 10 * 1024. Attachments ignore max_attachment_size_kb (users can submit files the server should reject, or are blocked below a higher attachment limit). Images are also capped at 10MB even when max_image_size_kb is larger, so previously allowed uploads are rejected. displayErrorForUpload's 413 branch (line 246) has the same hardcode and will report 10MB even when the real limit is different.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same problem described in the golden comment: hardcoding the upload size limit to 10 * 1024 instead of using `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, which breaks per-type and server-configured limits, and also notes the same issue in the 413 error handler.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated GIF downsize is passed a percentage geometry

When SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails is on and the file is a GIF, downsize uses gifsicle --resize-fit with the geometry "80%". gifsicle's --resize-fit expects pixel dimensions such as WIDTHxHEIGHT, not an ImageMagick percentage. Those attempts fail (convert_with returns false), the bytes are not reduced, and animated uploads that are over max_image_size_kb are never actually downsized.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: passing '80%' as dimensions to the downsize function fails for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is enabled because gifsicle's --resize-fit expects WxH geometry rather than a percentage.

false_positives.candidate:
ImageMagick downsize reads and writes the same path

OptimizedImage.downsize is called with tempfile.path as both the source and the destination. convert_with shells out to ImageMagick `convert` (and ImageOptim) with those paths. ImageMagick truncates the output file before it finishes reading the input, so using one path for both commonly yields an empty or corrupt file. The upload then proceeds with that damaged tempfile, so large-image downsizing fails or stores a broken image instead of a reduced original.

Downsize result is ignored and may never meet the size limit

The loop calls OptimizedImage.downsize but discards its false return value, and -resize 80% changes pixel dimensions rather than targeting a byte size. If convert fails, the file is unchanged or corrupt and the loop still retries the same path. If it succeeds, five 80% passes (about 33% of each side) often leave a JPEG/PNG larger than SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb. The code then always calls Upload.create_for on whatever is left, so an upload that the client just allowed can still be over the configured limit or be a failed conversion, with no error from this step.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing TopicUser crashes unsubscribe

unsubscribe does TopicUser.find_by(...) and then calls tu.notification_level with no nil check. Users can be emailed about a topic without an existing topic_users row (or the row can be absent for other reasons). Clicking the new email link then raises NoMethodError instead of unsubscribing, so the feature 500s for exactly the people the link is meant to serve. Use TopicUser.change, which creates the row when missing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: `TopicUser.find_by` can return nil if no record exists, and subsequently calling methods on the `tu` variable without a nil check will cause a crash (NoMethodError / nil pointer exception).

false_positives.candidate:
Unsubscribe is a GET that mutates notification level

TopicsController#unsubscribe is routed as GET /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe and immediately writes TopicUser.notification_level. Mail clients, link scanners, and antivirus gateways prefetch URLs in notification emails, so merely receiving or opening the message can change the recipient's topic notification level. The action is also not idempotent: a watching or tracking user is first dropped to regular, and a refresh or second prefetch then mutes them. State changes from an email link need a POST (or a single-use token) and must not keep downgrading on repeat requests.

Direct save leaves unsubscribe reversible by auto-track

The new action assigns notification_level and calls tu.save! instead of TopicUser.change. change sets notifications_reason_id to user_changed and notifications_changed_at, and publishes the level change. A raw save leaves notifications_reason_id nil. update_last_read then auto-promotes the user back to tracking whenever total time viewed exceeds the auto-track threshold, silently undoing the unsubscribe on the next visit or timing update. The open topic UI also never receives the MessageBus notification_level_change.

Preloaded topic JSON still has the old notification level

TopicView is built before the TopicUser row is updated, and perform_show_response serializes that same @topic_view into the preloaded topic payload. The notifications control on the page therefore still shows watching/tracking/regular after the server has already changed the level. The user is told notifications have stopped while the button shows the previous state, and using that button can write the stale level back.

Watching users are not actually unsubscribed

If notification_level is above regular (tracking or watching), the action sets regular instead of muted. Watching is the level that emails every reply, and the new server string says the link will "stop receiving notifications about this particular topic." After one click a watcher is still at regular, so mentions and replies-to-you still notify, and the client copy ("You will stop receiving notifications") is shown unconditionally. Only a second request mutes them, which is not what the email promises.

Unsubscribe template is not registered for its route

The Ember route is declared as topicUnsubscribe (templates/topic-unsubscribe, controller topic-unsubscribe). This file lives at templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs, which Ember resolves only for a nested topic.unsubscribe route. After the full-page load boots the app, the topicUnsubscribe route has no template, so the confirmation text and topic-notifications-button never render. Move the template to topic-unsubscribe.hbs (or nest the route under topic and point it at this template).

No coverage for the unsubscribe action

The only spec change passes unsubscribe_url into MessageBuilder and still does not assert that the topic link is rendered. There is no request/controller spec for TopicsController#unsubscribe: missing TopicUser, watching vs regular vs muted, repeat requests, slug redirect, or that the preloaded payload matches the saved level. Those paths are easy to regress and currently untested.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Empty updateMany does not bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt and can throw

fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache now calls SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {}) specifically to refresh SelectedCalendar.updatedAt after writing calendar cache. true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Webhook tunnel script is macOS-only and writes the wrong .env

sed -i '' is BSD sed syntax and fails on GNU sed (Linux). ENV_FILE is ../.env relative to the process cwd, not the script directory, so bash scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh from the repo root creates or edits a .env outside the repository instead of the app env file. The script then reports success while GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL was never set where the app reads it.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same problem described in the golden comment: that `sed -i ''` is BSD/macOS-specific syntax and will fail on Linux (GNU sed). Although the candidate also mentions an additional issue regarding the `.env` file path, it clearly captures the expected issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting cache does not refresh connected-calendar status

deleteCacheMutation only toasts and calls the optional onSuccess callback. Unlike the disconnect mutation in the same component, it never invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars. The settings page passes onChanged through, which is often undefined and is not the connectedCalendars query. After a successful delete the dropdown still renders the previous cacheUpdatedAt and still offers “Delete cached data” until a full reload.

Backfill stamps every existing cache row as updated at deploy time

The new NOT NULL updatedAt column is added with DEFAULT NOW() and no backfill from a real write time. Every pre-existing CalendarCache row, including expired ones, gets the migration timestamp. getCacheStatusByCredentialIds then takes MAX(updatedAt) with no expiresAt filter, so the new UI shows “Last updated” as the deploy time and treats expired legacy cache as present for every credential that has ever had a row.

No tests for cache deletion authorization or status query

deleteCache is an authenticated mutation that deletes every CalendarCache row for a credential after a userId ownership check, and connected calendars now depend on getCacheStatusByCredentialIds. true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex no longer serializes builds of the same key

BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the whole build, which also prevented two callers from indexing the same NamespacedResource at once. The lock is now taken only to insert the finished index. getOrCreateIndex is still check-then-act (GetIndex nil, then build), and init runs builds with an errgroup, so two builds of one key can overlap. The later insert overwrites the cache: the discarded index may already have watch updates applied, and the winner is a stale snapshot, so search silently misses writes. For file indexes, a second bleve.New on the same directory can also fail or corrupt the on-disk index. Per-key singleflight (or a lock held from the nil check through cache insert) is required; a shorter global lock alone does not fix the lost-update window.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: narrowing cacheMu protection from the entire BuildIndex operation to only the final cache insertion allows concurrent builds of the same index key. The candidate adds potential consequences and fixes, but its underlying issue matches the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs ranges the index cache without cacheMu

TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no lock. search.init now starts the watch goroutine and then immediately calls TotalDocs for the new startup log. That goroutine can handle a write for a namespace that was not prebuilt and call BuildIndex, which writes b.cache under cacheMu. Concurrent map iteration and write panics the process during startup. TotalDocs must take cacheMu.RLock (and BuildIndex must keep the write lock around the map update).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization while the newly started watcher can invoke BuildIndex and write to the cache, potentially causing a concurrent map iteration/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Startup watch starts at latest RV and drops events written during index build

init lists each namespace via build(), which returns the resource version observed by that list, then ignores it. Only after every namespace has been indexed does it call WatchWriteEvents, which records listLatestRVs at that later moment and polls strictly after those versions. Any write committed after a namespace's list snapshot and before the watch baseline (other storage-server replicas, or the main Grafana process writing the same DB while this process is still starting) is neither in the built index nor replayed. Moving this work into NewResourceServer makes that window the entire startup index build. The watch must resume from the RV returned by each build, not from the RV at the end of all builds.

Index init goroutines race on shared err and counter

The errgroup workers in init all assign the outer err from build() and increment totalBatchesIndexed with no synchronization. With WorkerThreads > 1 (the concurrency this change is trying to use), that is a data race: a worker can return another worker's nil and hide a failed namespace build, so Init succeeds while that index was never built. The span attribute namespaced_indexed is also racy. Each worker needs its own error variable, and the counter needs atomic increment or a post-Wait tally.

false_positives.candidate:
Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure

FixedQueuePool builds each queue.Queue() with the default maxsize (unlimited), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit always returns after put(). The class comment claims natural backpressure, but Arroyo will keep polling Kafka and enqueueing as fast as the broker allows. A single slow group blocks commits for its whole partition (offsets cannot advance past the oldest incomplete offset), while every later message on that partition is retained in memory. A hot or stuck subscription can therefore grow process memory without bound and turn the clog this PR is meant to avoid into an OOM, without ever pausing the consumer.

Strategy close kills the shared worker pool and stops commits before drain

The queue pool and its worker threads are created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and shared by every strategy from create_with_partitions. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets the commit-loop shutdown event, joins that thread, then calls FixedQueuePool.shutdown(). shutdown() sets each worker's shutdown flag before Queue.shutdown(), so a worker blocked in get() exits on ShutDown and does not drain remaining items, and a worker between iterations leaves the loop immediately. Offsets finished only during that drain are never committed because the commit thread is already stopped. On partition revoke/rebalance Arroyo closes this strategy and calls create_with_partitions again; the new strategy reuses the already-shut-down pool, so later messages are not processed for the rest of the process lifetime. join() also ignores its timeout and can block about 5s plus 5s per worker.

Kafka commits are invoked from a background thread

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls commit_function (the Arroyo commit callback, which reaches the librdkafka consumer) every second. Every other strategy in this consumer commits from the processing thread. librdkafka consumers are not thread-safe, and that callback races with poll, submit, and close/terminate on the main thread. terminate() does not even join the commit thread, so a commit can run while the consumer is shutting down. This can crash the consumer, commit a torn offset map, or lose the in-flight commit.

Failed messages are acked and never retried

OrderedQueueWorker.complete_offset runs in a finally block, including after result_processor raises, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit also add+completes the offset when decode, grouping, or put fails. The strategy docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing, but any exception is logged and then treated as done, with no DLQ on the uptime-results consumer. A transient DB or downstream failure is therefore committed (offset+1) and will not be redelivered, so an uptime check that failed to be handled can be dropped permanently. The new error-handling test asserts the opposite (no commit) and only sleeps 0.2s while the commit loop waits 1s, so it neither matches the code nor reliably checks it.

Queue-depth test races the workers and can flake

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts get_stats()['total_items'] > 0. Workers are already running and the processor is a no-op, so the queues can be empty before that assertion. test_different_groups_distributed likewise requires 20 hashed keys to land in all 3 buckets, which is not guaranteed. Both can fail on a quiet CI run without a product bug.

Span segment keys (span-buf:s:...) change from Redis sets (SADD/SUNIONSTORE/SSCAN) to sorted sets (ZADD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN/ZPOPMIN) without a new key prefix or migration. Keys written before deploy remain SETs until redis_ttl (default 3600s). Any Z* command against those keys returns WRONGTYPE, so process_spans and flush_segments fail for in-flight segments and those spans are dropped or stuck until TTL. A rolling deploy cannot safely mix old and new consumers on the same keys.

Segments over 1000 spans are silently truncated

After merge, the script ZPOPMINs span_count-1000 members (lowest end_timestamp_precise) with no metric or log. The flush path used to skip an oversized segment, increment spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded, and log; that check was removed from SpansBuffer._load_segment_data. If the same payload is already in both keys (retry, or the Python ZADD and a previous buffer both holding it), the merged score becomes the sum of end timestamps. zpopmin then treats that span as newest or oldest incorrectly and can drop a different span than the oldest one. sunionstore did not have scores, so this is a new failure mode of the set-to-zset conversion.

The parent-redirect loop now stops after 1000 hops (previously 10000, with a comment that deeper segment trees would not join). When the cap is hit, the span is attached to an intermediate set_span_id instead of the true segment root. true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful Delete records the object name as the metric kind label

On the Delete success path, recordStorageDuration is called with name (the object name) where every other call passes options.Kind. If that argument is a Prometheus label, each deleted object creates a new series and cardinality grows without bound. The error path on the previous line correctly uses options.Kind, so success and failure are also not comparable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same inconsistency: the Delete success path passes the object name to metrics recording instead of options.Kind, unlike other calls. The candidate adds potential consequences but matches the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled on return

Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s). That child is still cancelled as soon as the incoming request context is cancelled, which happens when the handler returns the unified-storage result. The 10s timeout never applies. The legacy "safe measure" write is therefore raced against request completion and will usually fail with context.Canceled, so legacy storage diverges from unified storage with no retry. Derive the background work from context.WithoutCancel (then apply the timeout), and log the legacy error instead of only recording a metric.

Legacy Update reuses the same UpdatedObjectInfo concurrently

After Storage.Update returns, the goroutine calls Legacy.Update with the same objInfo value. UpdatedObjectInfo implementations typically cache the computed object or mutate internal state on the first UpdatedObject call, and Storage.Update may still be using that state. Running both updates at once races on that shared object and no longer writes the unified-storage result into legacy (the previous code snapshotted the updated object and applied that exact object to legacy). Legacy can fail optimistic concurrency, apply a different patch, or panic, so the two stores diverge.

Storage failures and legacy delete-collection are recorded on the wrong histogram

Create and Update record a storage error with recordLegacyDuration (lines 45 and 129), so a unified-storage failure is counted as a legacy-storage failure and is missing from the storage histogram. DeleteCollection's async legacy call (line 166) uses recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency and errors are attributed to unified storage. Mode 3 latency/error dashboards will be wrong and can hide a broken legacy backfill.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy goroutines

Destroy closes Storage and Legacy immediately while Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection may still be running legacy writes in detached goroutines. Those calls can hit a destroyed backend (panic or lost write) during shutdown or mode switch, and there is no way for the caller to know the backfill finished.

Mode 3 tests never observe the async legacy write and mock the wrong store on errors

The Create error case is named as a unified-storage failure but only stubs Legacy.Create, and Storage.Create has no expectation, so the test does not exercise the path it claims. Success cases start legacy work in a goroutine and return without AssertCalled, a wait, or AssertExpectations, so a missing or panicked legacy write still passes. The playlist mode 3 integration test then reads the legacy API immediately after a k8s write, which will flake or fail for the same unsynchronized async path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Federated rules are always treated as editable

useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false (the old isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) check is gone, and RuleGroupIdentifierV2 cannot express source_tenants). Federated Mimir/GEM groups were previously immutable. Every consumer of useAlertRuleAbility / useAllAlertRuleAbilities will now offer edit, delete, pause, and duplicate on federated rules.

Delete is unreachable in the ruler-free list view

canDelete can be true from useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities when only a Prometheus rule is loaded, but the Delete item is still rendered only when rulerRule is defined, and onClick passes that rulerRule to handleDelete. GrafanaRuleListItem never supplies a ruler rule, and RuleActionsButtons already deletes via the identifier (showDeleteModal(identifier, groupIdentifier)), so the extra guard hides Delete for every Grafana rule in the new list. The group-loader menu test even asserts only four items and never looks for Delete despite granting AlertingRuleDelete.

Pause never appears without a ruler rule

canPause is OR-ed with the Prometheus-rule ability so the list view can authorize pause without the ruler API, but the menu item is still gated on rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) and MenuItemPauseRule requires a RulerGrafanaRuleDTO. In the new list, rulerRule is undefined, so Pause is never shown even for users who can edit the rule.

Recording-rule export and pause dropped

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities sets ModifyExport, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently supported only when prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. The ruler path used rulerRuleType.grafana.rule, which includes Grafana recording rules. Recording rules in the list therefore lose export and pause/restore even when the user has folder edit permission and the rule is not provisioned.

Rule view links drop returnTo

The removed GrafanaRuleListItem built the view href with createReturnTo() so the detail page could navigate back to the current list URL (including filters). The replacement always links to /alerting/grafana/${uid}/view with no returnTo query. Opening a rule from the list no longer restores the filtered list on back navigation.

Interpolating before the $__range guard splits queries that must stay whole

runSplitQuery now runs datasource.applyTemplateVariables before querySupportsSplitting. That helper refuses to split expressions that still contain [$__range], [$__range_s], or [$__range_ms], because those macros must be resolved against the original request range (the comment says backend interpolation on a split range is wrong). templateSrv.replace, which applyTemplateVariables uses, substitutes $__range* from the parent request before that check, so isQueryWithRangeVariable no longer matches and the query is day-split. Each chunk is then executed with the full-dashboard duration already baked in (for example [7d] on a 1-day window), which over-counts range aggregations and multiplies Loki load. The same substitution also happens in runShardSplitQuery before it delegates to runSplitQuery, so the shard path has the same hole.

Pre-interpolating range vars breaks stream-shard selector rewrite

runShardSplitQuery now expands variables with applyTemplateVariables before interpolateShardingSelector rewrites the stream selector (line 154). interpolateShardingSelector inserts the shard matcher and `| drop __stream_shard__` by replacing the `{...}` selector only. If a range like [$__auto] is still attached to that selector, the rewrite keeps a valid range vector; after this change [$__auto] is already `5m`, so the range is left behind the inserted pipeline. The new test locks in the result: `count_over_time({a="b", __stream_shard__=~"20|10"} | drop __stream_shard__[5m])`, which is invalid LogQL (count_over_time requires a range vector, and [5m] is bound to the drop stage). Sharded metric queries whose range or step is a variable will fail or return errors.

applyTemplateVariables runs again on already interpolated shard requests

runShardSplitQuery already maps every target through applyTemplateVariables(query, scopedVars, request.filters) and then calls runSplitQuery on each shard subrequest. runSplitQuery applies the same function again, still passing request.filters. applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent when filters are present: ad-hoc matchers are appended to expr on every call, so each sharded subquery gets duplicate label matchers and can be rejected by Loki. The updated shard test expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times (once up front plus once per group inside runSplitQuery), which confirms the re-entry, but nothing asserts that filters or escaped matchers survive a second pass.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is not atomic with the insert

CreateOrUpdateDevice reads CountDevices and, only if the count is still under deviceLimit, performs a separate INSERT. Those steps are not in one transaction and are not serialized with the existing server lock, so concurrent anonymous requests (including across Grafana replicas sharing the database) can all observe count < limit and all insert. The configured cap can be exceeded by the number of in-flight creates, and nothing in the schema enforces the limit.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify a race condition caused by a non-atomic device count check followed by insertion, allowing concurrent requests to exceed the device limit without transaction or lock protection.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit is bypassed after the first request

tagDeviceUI writes the device cache key before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns. When the store is at the limit, a new device's first TagDevice call fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached (so Authenticate denies that request), but the key is already cached for 29 minutes. Every later request for that device ID hits the cache and returns nil without touching the database, so anonymous authentication succeeds and the device is never counted. The configured limit therefore only fails a single attempt per device per cache TTL and does not actually cap anonymous access.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device ID before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, leaving the entry cached after ErrDeviceLimitReached and allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit for the 29-minute cache TTL.

false_positives.candidate:

AnonymousDeviceLimit is read from auth.anonymous device_limit (default 0, meaning unlimited), but this change does not add the key to defaults.ini / sample.ini or any docs. Operators have no documented way to discover the setting, its default, or that 0 disables enforcement, so the feature cannot be configured as intended.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are not loaded before translate caches a miss

I18n.translate only calls load_locale for config.locale, and the new fallback chain (site default locale, then :en) is loaded solely from ApplicationController#set_locale via I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. Any I18n.t outside that filter—mailers, jobs, models, middleware, or a request that translates before set_locale—looks up fallbacks whose YAML was never loaded. The accelerator then freezes that result in the process-wide LRU (including the default missing-translation string). Later requests that do load :en still serve the cached miss until the entry is evicted or the process restarts, so users see raw keys instead of the intended site-locale or English fallback.

Translation cache ignores the site fallback locale

The LRU key is only key + I18n.locale + backend object_id. FallbackLocaleList resolves misses using SiteSetting.default_locale, but that value is not part of the key and nothing clears @cache when the setting changes. After an admin changes the site default locale, strings already resolved through the old fallback stay cached for each user locale, so the UI keeps showing the previous language until restart or an unrelated I18n.reload!.

Every fallback lookup reads SiteSetting.default_locale

Backend::Fallbacks calls I18n.fallbacks[locale] on each translate, and FallbackLocaleList#[] unconditionally calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym. That runs for every I18n.t once this initializer is loaded, including asset precompile, migrations, and boot paths where the settings store/DB is not available. Those tasks previously did not enable i18n fallbacks (the flag lived only in production/profile). They can now raise while building the fallback list, and a nil default_locale raises NoMethodError on to_sym instead of degrading to :en.

No tests for fallback order or lazy locale loading

The custom chain (requested locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en), the move of fallbacks out of the environment configs, and ensure_loaded! are untested. A regression that drops :en, skips loading a fallback file, or caches a miss would ship unnoticed, which is exactly the failure mode this change introduces next to the translate accelerator.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).
