false_positives.candidate:
Member item template looks up a block variable that itemView does not define

group.hbs renders members with `{{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}`, and this item template then uses `member` (`{{avatar member}}`, `{{member.username}}`, `{{action "removeMember" member}}`). An Ember itemView's context is the user record itself; the `each` block variable is not in scope inside `templateName`. Username and avatar therefore render blank, and removeMember is invoked with undefined, so the DELETE is sent without a user id (or not at all). The template should bind `username` / `this` (or `view.content`) on the item context.

remove_member deletes by raw id and skips Group#remove

`group.users.delete(user_id)` passes an Integer. On the Rails 4.1 association API this app uses, `has_many#delete` type-checks each argument and raises `ActiveRecord::AssociationTypeMismatch` unless the value is a User, so every removal 500s and the membership is unchanged (the new spec would fail). Even on a Rails version that accepts ids, `delete` skips `Group#remove` / GroupUser callbacks that the old patch path used, so counter caches and primary-group cleanup are not run. Load the user and call `group.remove(user)`.

Creating a group drops alias_level

`create` only assigns `name` and `visible`. The admin form shows the alias-level combo before the group has an id, and `Group#asJSON` / `Group#create` send `alias_level`, but the controller never reads it. A group created with "everyone" or "mods and admins" is stored at the column default (nobody) until a later update. `update` already applies `params[:alias_level]`; `create` needs the same assignment.

members offset/limit are not clamped

`offset = params[:offset].to_i` is passed straight to SQL. A negative offset (easy to send, and the client can also land past the end after the last member of a page is removed because the server echoes the requested offset) makes PostgreSQL raise `OFFSET must not be negative` and turns the members request into a 500. Limit is also unbounded, so `?limit=` can force the public members endpoint to load an entire automatic group (trust_level_0) into one response. Clamp offset to `>= 0` and to the last page, and cap limit.

Add/remove membership failures are swallowed

`removeMember` and `addMembers` only chain `.then` to reload the list. A 422 (automatic group, validation error) or network failure never surfaces a message, unlike `save`/`destroy` which bootbox the error. The admin UI keeps the old member list with no indication the change did not stick.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Block check writes stats and is counted twice per signup

should_block? increments match_count and saves last_match_at as a side effect of validation, using a non-atomic read-modify-write. UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save, and save validates again, so one signup attempt runs EmailValidator twice and advances match_count by 2. Concurrent attempts can also lose updates. last_match_at and match_count therefore do not record how many times the address was actually submitted, which breaks the statistic this table is added to track.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: the block-check method mutates statistics during a read-like operation, using non-atomic updates that can cause concurrency problems. The double-counting during signup is an additional consequence of those side effects.

true_positives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Domain allow/deny regex is unanchored

email_in_restriction_setting? builds Regexp.new("@(#{domains})") and tests it with =~, with no end anchor and with only "." escaped. A blacklist entry of "gmail.com" therefore matches "user@gmail.com.evil.test" as well as the real domain, and a whitelist entry likewise treats that host as allowed. Attackers can evade the domain blacklist (and pass a whitelist) by appending another label, so the restriction this validator is supposed to enforce does not hold.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying bug: email_in_restriction_setting? uses an inadequately anchored domain regex, allowing unintended domains to match restriction entries. The candidate describes a different malicious hostname example but points to the same missing domain-boundary enforcement.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and unnormalized

BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the address with an exact BlockedEmail.where(email: email) match, and neither this method nor EmailValidator downcases or strips the value first. PostgreSQL's unique index is also case-sensitive, so a row stored as "bad@spam.com" will not match a signup of "Bad@spam.com" or " bad@spam.com". The block is therefore bypassed by trivial casing or whitespace changes, and the new blocked-email control does not actually stop the address it was meant to stop.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same case-sensitive lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? that allows differently capitalized versions of a blocked email address to bypass the block. Its additional whitespace concern does not change the core match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Header panel right alignment fails outside modern flex

.panel no longer uses float: right. Right alignment is only margin-left: auto plus order(3), and .d-header .contents is a flex container via the new mixin (including display: -webkit-box / -ms-flexbox). Auto margins do not absorb free space in the 2009 -webkit-box model those prefixes turn on, and in any browser that ignores display: flex the panel is a normal block whose auto margin computes to 0. The icons, login, and sign-up controls then stay on the left under the logo instead of the right side of the header. The prefixed mixin does not provide a float fallback for the technique that replaced float: right.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the loss of the panel's float:right fallback when alignment is replaced by flex-dependent styling, causing the panel to appear left-aligned or below the title when it is not a flex item. The candidate emphasizes browser compatibility rather than the non-Ember/noscript structure, but describes the same underlying alignment regression.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order mixin uses one number for 0-based and 1-based flex specs

@mixin order writes the same $val to -webkit-box-ordinal-group, -ms-flex-order, and order. -webkit-box-ordinal-group is 1-based (initial value 1; 0 is invalid) while order and -ms-flex-order are 0-based (initial value 0). Call sites pass order(2) on .extra-info-wrapper and order(3) on .panel. In old WebKit those become ordinal groups 2 and 3 against siblings that stay at the default of 1, so source order among any items that should share a slot will not match modern flex, and a later order(0) or order(1) would be dropped or tied with defaults. The prefixed value needs to be $val + 1 for -webkit-box-ordinal-group.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same indexing mismatch: legacy box-ordinal-group requires values starting at 1, while order accepts 0. It explicitly notes that order(0) is invalid in old WebKit and proposes adding 1. Omitting the Mozilla prefix does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Flex on .small-action drops the right-aligned action button

.small-action is now a flex container, but the action button is still only positioned with float: right (and .topic-avatar with float: left). Float is ignored on flex items, and .small-action-desc is left at the default flex: 0 1 auto with padding changed from 0.5em 0 0.5em 4em to 0 1.5%. The description therefore shrink-wraps its text instead of filling the row, and the button sits immediately after the label instead of on the far right of the post action. The old 4em left padding was what kept text clear of the avatar in the float layout; 1.5% of a shrink-wrapped flex item is effectively no gap, so avatar and text also collide or sit flush. Give the description flex-grow (and a real gap) and push the button with margin-left: auto, or do not make this row a flex container while it still depends on floats.

Custom action message paragraphs lose vertical separation

.small-action .custom-message p margin was changed from 5px 0 to 0 as part of the flex alignment tweak. That rule is the spacing between paragraphs inside the moderator/small-action custom message, which is not a flex item and is not centered by align-items on .small-action. Multi-paragraph action descriptions now render as a single unspaced block.

Header flex items cannot shrink, so long titles push the panel off-screen

.d-header .contents is display: flex with no min-width: 0, overflow, or flex-shrink override on its children. Flex items default to min-width: auto, so they will not shrink below their content. .extra-info-wrapper (order 2, the docked topic title) and the logo title sit in that row with .panel (margin-left: auto, order 3). A long topic title therefore forces the row wider than the viewport and shoves the header icons off-screen instead of ellipsizing, which the previous float layout did not do. Set min-width: 0 and overflow/text-overflow on the title/extra-info flex items.

false_negatives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
website_name bypasses TL0 field hiding

include_website_name is never consulted: ActiveModel::Serializer only calls include_website_name?. website_name is also missing from untrusted_attributes, unlike website. Anonymous viewers of a TL0 user therefore still get website_name (host, and host+path when it matches the instance), which is the same profile URL the serializer is supposed to withhold. The new specs never cover a TL0/anonymous viewer, so this leak is untested.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing '?' suffix on include_website_name and explains that the serializer therefore never consults it for conditional inclusion. Although it adds a privacy consequence and does not mention string-literal mutation, it matches the golden comment's primary underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
Same-domain path display fails on case and www

Hosts are compared case-sensitively and without normalizing a leading www. A site at example.com will not treat http://Example.com/user or http://www.example.com/user as the same domain (lengths differ, and example.com does not end with .www.example.com), so the profile shows only the host. The inverse (instance on www, website on the apex) does append the path, so the feature is inconsistent with its own parent-domain rule. Comparisons should downcase both hosts and treat a single www label as equivalent before deciding whether to append the path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Resize messages accepted from any origin that is a substring of discourseUrl

The check is `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1`, not an equality check against the forum origin. Any `e.origin` that appears inside `discourseUrl` is trusted. For example `http://localhost` matches `http://localhost:3000`, and a short prefix such as `https://forum` matches `https://forum.example.com`. A page on that origin can post a `discourse-resize` message and set the iframe height.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying vulnerability: origin validation uses indexOf substring matching rather than exact origin equality, allowing messages from unintended origins. The differing bypass examples do not change the core issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin is a full referer URL

`parent.postMessage(..., '<%= request.referer %>')` passes the full referer (scheme, host, path, and query). `postMessage` requires an origin (`scheme://host[:port]`) or `*`. A path-bearing referer throws, so the parent never receives `discourse-resize` and the iframe stays at its default height.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: passing the full referrer URL as postMessage's targetOrigin instead of just the origin prevents the resize message from reaching the parent. The differing description of how delivery fails does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Imported URL is interpolated into HTML unsafely The imported-from footer builds `#{url}` from the source URL after only checking that it starts with http/https. A URL containing a quote or other markup (for example `http://evil.test/' onclick='alert(1)`) breaks out of the attribute. Combined with the raw_html cook path, that markup is stored and rendered as HTML.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same XSS vulnerability caused by interpolating an unescaped URL into the generated HTML. It does not mention the nil-contents NoMethodError, but directly matches the security issue described in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Embed template has invalid ERB and will not render

`<%- end if %>` is not valid ERB/Ruby (it must be `<% end %>`). Rendering `embed/best` raises a syntax error, so every successful embed that already has a topic returns 500 instead of the discussion iframe.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the invalid ERB/Ruby closing statement `end if`, which causes a render-time syntax error and should be replaced with `end`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed poll crashes when an item has no content

`i.content.scrub` assumes every SimpleRSS item has an HTML `content` string. RSS 2.0 items usually only have `description`, and `content` is nil, so the hourly job raises NoMethodError and imports nothing. `CGI.unescapeHTML` on that body also turns escaped markup (`<script>`) into live tags before it is stored as raw HTML.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: calling `i.content.scrub` when RSS items lack content causes a nil-related crash, and description is the available alternative. The additional HTML concern does not negate the match.

false_positives.candidate:
raw_html posts skip cooking and sanitization

When `cook_method` is `raw_html`, `cook` returns `raw` unchanged and never runs the normal pipeline or Sanitize. Feed and readability imports store that HTML as the post body (`TopicEmbed.import` sets this cook method and `skip_validations: true`). The embed view then emits it with `raw post.cooked`, and the forum will too. A feed item or fetched page can therefore inject script/markup that runs on the Discourse origin for anyone who views the topic or the embed.

Embed controller spec expects a retriever the action never calls

The example stubs `TopicRetriever.new` and expects `#retrieve` when no embed exists. `EmbedController#best` only calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)`. That expectation fails, so the new controller spec does not pass and does not actually cover the enqueue path, referer/host mismatch, or the loading template.

embed_url is limited to 255 characters

`t.string :embed_url` uses the default varchar(255) and a unique index. Article and feed URLs with long paths or query strings exceed that and `TopicEmbed.create!` fails, so those pages never embed and the retrieve job errors instead of importing.

Each cache miss synchronously polls the entire feed

`perform_retrieve` calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline whenever feed polling is enabled and this URL is not yet embedded. That opens the feed with no timeout and imports every item on the request/job that is only trying to fetch one URL. A slow or huge feed blocks the worker, and many distinct embed URLs repeat the full poll.

Any embed_url is enqueued after a spoofable referer check

Host allowlisting happens only later in `TopicRetriever`, not before `Jobs.enqueue`. The referer check uses a client-supplied header, so a caller can set `Referer` to the configured host and enqueue `retrieve_topic` for arbitrary `embed_url` values. That floods the job queue; URLs that do match `embeddable_host` are then fetched server-side with `open` (no timeout, redirects followed).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second downsize definition overwrites the width/height API

Ruby does not overload methods. The new downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts) at this line replaces the downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts) defined just above, so that width/height implementation is dead. Existing callers that pass numeric max width and height now treat the width as a geometry string and the height integer as opts. optimize then evaluates opts[:allow_animation] and raises NoMethodError, so thumbnail downsizing that still uses the old signature breaks.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the second downsize definition overrides the first, making the separate width/height implementation unreachable and breaking callers using the original signature. The candidate adds details about the resulting failure but describes the same underlying bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upload size cap hardcoded to 10MB for every type

validateUploadedFile used to enforce Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so images and attachments had separate admin-configured limits. It now always uses 10 * 1024. Attachments ignore max_attachment_size_kb (users can submit files the server should reject, or are blocked below a higher attachment limit). Images are also capped at 10MB even when max_image_size_kb is larger, so previously allowed uploads are rejected. displayErrorForUpload's 413 branch (line 246) has the same hardcode and will report 10MB even when the real limit is different.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same hardcoded 10MB limit replacing per-type Discourse.SiteSettings limits, causing client/server discrepancies, and explicitly includes the same hardcode in the 413 error handler.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated GIF downsize is passed a percentage geometry

When SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails is on and the file is a GIF, downsize uses gifsicle --resize-fit with the geometry "80%". gifsicle's --resize-fit expects pixel dimensions such as WIDTHxHEIGHT, not an ImageMagick percentage. Those attempts fail (convert_with returns false), the bytes are not reduced, and animated uploads that are over max_image_size_kb are never actually downsized.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: animated GIF downsizing passes "80%" to gifsicle --resize-fit, which requires WxH geometry, causing downsizing to fail when allow_animated_thumbnails is enabled.

false_positives.candidate:
ImageMagick downsize reads and writes the same path

OptimizedImage.downsize is called with tempfile.path as both the source and the destination. convert_with shells out to ImageMagick `convert` (and ImageOptim) with those paths. ImageMagick truncates the output file before it finishes reading the input, so using one path for both commonly yields an empty or corrupt file. The upload then proceeds with that damaged tempfile, so large-image downsizing fails or stores a broken image instead of a reduced original.

Downsize result is ignored and may never meet the size limit

The loop calls OptimizedImage.downsize but discards its false return value, and -resize 80% changes pixel dimensions rather than targeting a byte size. If convert fails, the file is unchanged or corrupt and the loop still retries the same path. If it succeeds, five 80% passes (about 33% of each side) often leave a JPEG/PNG larger than SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb. The code then always calls Upload.create_for on whatever is left, so an upload that the client just allowed can still be over the configured limit or be a failed conversion, with no error from this step.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing TopicUser crashes unsubscribe

unsubscribe does TopicUser.find_by(...) and then calls tu.notification_level with no nil check. Users can be emailed about a topic without an existing topic_users row (or the row can be absent for other reasons). Clicking the new email link then raises NoMethodError instead of unsubscribing, so the feature 500s for exactly the people the link is meant to serve. Use TopicUser.change, which creates the row when missing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same nil dereference: when no TopicUser record exists, tu is nil and calling tu.notification_level crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
Unsubscribe is a GET that mutates notification level

TopicsController#unsubscribe is routed as GET /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe and immediately writes TopicUser.notification_level. Mail clients, link scanners, and antivirus gateways prefetch URLs in notification emails, so merely receiving or opening the message can change the recipient's topic notification level. The action is also not idempotent: a watching or tracking user is first dropped to regular, and a refresh or second prefetch then mutes them. State changes from an email link need a POST (or a single-use token) and must not keep downgrading on repeat requests.

Direct save leaves unsubscribe reversible by auto-track

The new action assigns notification_level and calls tu.save! instead of TopicUser.change. change sets notifications_reason_id to user_changed and notifications_changed_at, and publishes the level change. A raw save leaves notifications_reason_id nil. update_last_read then auto-promotes the user back to tracking whenever total time viewed exceeds the auto-track threshold, silently undoing the unsubscribe on the next visit or timing update. The open topic UI also never receives the MessageBus notification_level_change.

Preloaded topic JSON still has the old notification level

TopicView is built before the TopicUser row is updated, and perform_show_response serializes that same @topic_view into the preloaded topic payload. The notifications control on the page therefore still shows watching/tracking/regular after the server has already changed the level. The user is told notifications have stopped while the button shows the previous state, and using that button can write the stale level back.

Watching users are not actually unsubscribed

If notification_level is above regular (tracking or watching), the action sets regular instead of muted. Watching is the level that emails every reply, and the new server string says the link will "stop receiving notifications about this particular topic." After one click a watcher is still at regular, so mentions and replies-to-you still notify, and the client copy ("You will stop receiving notifications") is shown unconditionally. Only a second request mutes them, which is not what the email promises.

Unsubscribe template is not registered for its route

The Ember route is declared as topicUnsubscribe (templates/topic-unsubscribe, controller topic-unsubscribe). This file lives at templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs, which Ember resolves only for a nested topic.unsubscribe route. After the full-page load boots the app, the topicUnsubscribe route has no template, so the confirmation text and topic-notifications-button never render. Move the template to topic-unsubscribe.hbs (or nest the route under topic and point it at this template).

No coverage for the unsubscribe action

The only spec change passes unsubscribe_url into MessageBuilder and still does not assert that the topic link is rendered. There is no request/controller spec for TopicsController#unsubscribe: missing TopicUser, watching vs regular vs muted, repeat requests, slug redirect, or that the preloaded payload matches the saved level. Those paths are easy to regress and currently untested.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Empty updateMany does not bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt and can throw

fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache now calls SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {}) specifically to refresh SelectedCalendar.updatedAt after writing calendar cache. Prisma only applies @updatedAt when the update payload changes at least one field; an empty data object is either a no-op (updatedAt stays stale) or an invalid updateMany invocation that throws. This runs on the Google webhook/cache-refresh path after the cache upsert, so a throw fails the refresh even though the cache write succeeded, and a no-op means the timestamp this change exists to maintain is never updated.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: passing an empty data object to updateManyByCredentialId prevents Prisma's @updatedAt behavior from refreshing the timestamp, leaving cache status tracking stale. Its additional claim about a possible exception does not change the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Webhook tunnel script is macOS-only and writes the wrong .env

sed -i '' is BSD sed syntax and fails on GNU sed (Linux). ENV_FILE is ../.env relative to the process cwd, not the script directory, so bash scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh from the repo root creates or edits a .env outside the repository instead of the app env file. The script then reports success while GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL was never set where the app reads it.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that `sed -i ''` uses macOS/BSD sed syntax and fails on GNU sed on Linux, matching the golden issue. The additional .env path concern does not negate this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting cache does not refresh connected-calendar status

deleteCacheMutation only toasts and calls the optional onSuccess callback. Unlike the disconnect mutation in the same component, it never invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars. The settings page passes onChanged through, which is often undefined and is not the connectedCalendars query. After a successful delete the dropdown still renders the previous cacheUpdatedAt and still offers “Delete cached data” until a full reload.

Backfill stamps every existing cache row as updated at deploy time

The new NOT NULL updatedAt column is added with DEFAULT NOW() and no backfill from a real write time. Every pre-existing CalendarCache row, including expired ones, gets the migration timestamp. getCacheStatusByCredentialIds then takes MAX(updatedAt) with no expiresAt filter, so the new UI shows “Last updated” as the deploy time and treats expired legacy cache as present for every credential that has ever had a row.

No tests for cache deletion authorization or status query

deleteCache is an authenticated mutation that deletes every CalendarCache row for a credential after a userId ownership check, and connected calendars now depend on getCacheStatusByCredentialIds. There are no tests for a matching owner, a credential owned by another user, a missing id, or the groupBy status mapping (including expired rows). A regression in the where clause would either 500 the calendar settings page or let one user wipe another user’s cache with no CI signal.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

If the weekday is absent from every entry, find returns undefined and the function falls through to the busy check and can return true, so a fixed host's day off is still bookable in round-robin. If several ranges share that weekday, the first range that does not contain the slot makes find succeed even when a later range does contain it, so a slot inside a second interval is rejected. end is also computed from the slot start minute, not slot start plus event length, so a meeting that starts inside hours and runs past workingHour.endTime is accepted.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
All-day block comparison never matches

The unavailable-all-day branch compares two Dayjs instances with ===. That checks object identity, not time, so dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...) is always false. A date override stored with equal start and end (the usual all-day unavailable marker) never takes this path and depends on the other window checks, which do not treat a zero-length range as blocking the whole day.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: comparing separately created Dayjs objects with === checks reference identity rather than date values, causing the comparison to always be false. The candidate adds impact details but describes the same underlying issue.

Date-override window check rejects valid slots and accepts partial overlaps

checkIfIsAvailable treats a slot as outside the date override if it is outside any one override range on that calendar day. dateOverrides.find returns the first range for which the slot ends before the range start or starts after the range end, and the caller then returns false. With two ranges on the same day (for example 09:00-11:00 and 14:00-16:00), a slot fully inside the first range is still rejected because it is outside the second. The inverse is also wrong: a slot that only partially overlaps a range does not hit either outside-condition, so it is treated as inside. Fixed-host round-robin days with more than one override, or slots that stick out of the override, are therefore bookable or hidden incorrectly.

Override match returns available before busy times are checked

If any date override exists on the slot's calendar day and the slot was not rejected by the window checks, checkIfIsAvailable returns true immediately. Busy calendar events, existing bookings, and buffers passed in busy are never consulted. A fixed host who set a date override can therefore be booked on top of a meeting that falls inside that override, which is a double-booking.

Override offset is reduced to clock time and can drop the range

After shifting the override by inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset, only .hour() and .minute() are kept. A shift across midnight is applied as minutes-on-the-same-invitee-day that passed the activeOverrides filter, so the window lands on the wrong clock time (and often the wrong date). If the end crosses midnight and the start does not, endTime becomes less than startTime and buildSlots skips the range with start >= end, so that date override disappears entirely for attendees in a timezone on the other side of midnight from the organizer.

The added getSchedule call asks for Asia/Dhaka but expects the same UTC slot list already asserted for Asia/Kolkata, and it uses a personal event with no hosts. It cannot fail if fixed-host date overrides are ignored in round-robin, if an override day still ignores busy time, or if the offset math moves slots across a date boundary. The PR's stated fixes (#8207 / fixed hosts, timezone-adjusted overrides) ship with no assertion that would catch the checkIfIsAvailable regressions.

The cron will keep selecting that reminder on every run until scheduledDate is in the past, which is the infinite reschedule this PR is meant to stop (for example a booking with no attendee phone number). false_positives.candidate:
Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure

FixedQueuePool builds each queue.Queue() with the default maxsize (unlimited), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit always returns after put(). The class comment claims natural backpressure, but Arroyo will keep polling Kafka and enqueueing as fast as the broker allows. A single slow group blocks commits for its whole partition (offsets cannot advance past the oldest incomplete offset), while every later message on that partition is retained in memory. A hot or stuck subscription can therefore grow process memory without bound and turn the clog this PR is meant to avoid into an OOM, without ever pausing the consumer.

Strategy close kills the shared worker pool and stops commits before drain

The queue pool and its worker threads are created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and shared by every strategy from create_with_partitions. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets the commit-loop shutdown event, joins that thread, then calls FixedQueuePool.shutdown(). shutdown() sets each worker's shutdown flag before Queue.shutdown(), so a worker blocked in get() exits on ShutDown and does not drain remaining items, and a worker between iterations leaves the loop immediately. Offsets finished only during that drain are never committed because the commit thread is already stopped. On partition revoke/rebalance Arroyo closes this strategy and calls create_with_partitions again; the new strategy reuses the already-shut-down pool, so later messages are not processed for the rest of the process lifetime. join() also ignores its timeout and can block about 5s plus 5s per worker.

Kafka commits are invoked from a background thread

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls commit_function (the Arroyo commit callback, which reaches the librdkafka consumer) every second. Every other strategy in this consumer commits from the processing thread. librdkafka consumers are not thread-safe, and that callback races with poll, submit, and close/terminate on the main thread. terminate() does not even join the commit thread, so a commit can run while the consumer is shutting down. This can crash the consumer, commit a torn offset map, or lose the in-flight commit.

Failed messages are acked and never retried

OrderedQueueWorker.complete_offset runs in a finally block, including after result_processor raises, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit also add+completes the offset when decode, grouping, or put fails. The strategy docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing, but any exception is logged and then treated as done, with no DLQ on the uptime-results consumer. A transient DB or downstream failure is therefore committed (offset+1) and will not be redelivered, so an uptime check that failed to be handled can be dropped permanently. The new error-handling test asserts the opposite (no commit) and only sleeps 0.2s while the commit loop waits 1s, so it neither matches the code nor reliably checks it.

Queue-depth test races the workers and can flake

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts get_stats()['total_items'] > 0. Workers are already running and the processor is a no-op, so the queues can be empty before that assertion. test_different_groups_distributed likewise requires 20 hashed keys to land in all 3 buckets, which is not guaranteed. Both can fail on a quiet CI run without a product bug.

false_positives.candidate:
In-place SET to ZSET change breaks existing span-buffer keys

Span segment keys (span-buf:s:...) change from Redis sets (SADD/SUNIONSTORE/SSCAN) to sorted sets (ZADD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN/ZPOPMIN) without a new key prefix or migration. Keys written before deploy remain SETs until redis_ttl (default 3600s). Any Z* command against those keys returns WRONGTYPE, so process_spans and flush_segments fail for in-flight segments and those spans are dropped or stuck until TTL. A rolling deploy cannot safely mix old and new consumers on the same keys.

Segments over 1000 spans are silently truncated

After merge, the script ZPOPMINs span_count-1000 members (lowest end_timestamp_precise) with no metric or log. The flush path used to skip an oversized segment, increment spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded, and log; that check was removed from SpansBuffer._load_segment_data. Truncated segments are still flushed and produced as if complete, so spans are lost with no signal, and the cap is hardcoded at 1000 rather than SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (1001). There is no test that a segment larger than the cap drops the oldest members and still flushes the rest.

ZUNIONSTORE sums scores and can evict the wrong spans

zunionstore is called without AGGREGATE MIN/MAX, so Redis defaults to SUM. If the same payload is already in both keys (retry, or the Python ZADD and a previous buffer both holding it), the merged score becomes the sum of end timestamps. zpopmin then treats that span as newest or oldest incorrectly and can drop a different span than the oldest one. sunionstore did not have scores, so this is a new failure mode of the set-to-zset conversion.

Redirect walk cap cut from 10000 to 1000

The parent-redirect loop now stops after 1000 hops (previously 10000, with a comment that deeper segment trees would not join). When the cap is hit, the span is attached to an intermediate set_span_id instead of the true segment root. Deep traces are flushed as multiple incomplete segments, and the warning comment that documented this limit was removed. No test covers a chain longer than the new cap.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Allowlist cache key is process-local and invalidation is never called

The eligibility cache key is built with hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))). Tuple hashing is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so workers do not share keys and invalidate_upsampling_cache deletes a different key than the one another process wrote. That helper is also never called when issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist changes, despite the docstring saying it must be. A False or True allowlist result is then reused for 60 seconds. The new stats tests patch options.get but not the cache, so a later case with the same project ids can still see the first case's cached True and fail or pass for the wrong reason.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. _get_event_stats decides upsampling with the closed-over dataset from get_dataset(request), then runs the query on scoped_dataset. Dashboard widget splitting calls this with discover (and an errors-only or transactions-only query) while the outer dataset is still metrics_performance or metrics_enhanced_performance. _should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns false for those metrics datasets, so the errors split never rewrites count(). The opposite also holds: an errors/discover request dataset can rewrite columns on a scoped dataset that is not the errors dataset. Counts for split dashboard widgets will be wrong or the rewritten function will be invalid on the dataset that actually runs.
true_positives.reasoning: Both report the same bug: the upsampling check uses the outer request dataset instead of scoped_dataset, so upsampling is skipped in dashboard split paths where discover runs but the request dataset is metrics.

false_positives.candidate:
Upsampled count sums the wrong field and does not invert sample rate

transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling rewrites count() to upsampled_count(), and the new SnQL function is sum(sample_weight) cast to int. The only ingest change, _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling, writes contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate onto sample_rate and never sets sample_weight. A client_sample_rate of 0.1 means the stored event represents about 10 events, but nothing computes 1/sample_rate, and the aggregate does not read sample_rate. Allowlisted error stats will either query a missing/zero sample_weight column (query error or a count of 0) or, if that column happens to hold the rate, return a fractional rate instead of an upsampled count. The new stats test expects count == 10 for one event at rate 0.1, which this path cannot produce.

Error-query detection is a substring match and treats exclusions as errors

_is_error_focused_query lowercases the raw query string and returns true if it contains the substring "event.type:error". That also matches negated or unrelated clauses such as "!event.type:error" and "event.type:error OR event.type:transaction". Discover queries that exclude errors are then rewritten from count() to upsampled_count()/sum(sample_weight). Transactions and other non-error events do not have that column, so those stats requests fail or return inflated/zero counts. The same check misses the dashboard errors split, which uses "!event.type:transaction" rather than "event.type:error", so genuine error-only discover queries are not upsampled.

upsampled_count is only registered on the discover dataset

The new upsampled_count SnQL function is added only inside DiscoverDataset.function_converter. is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects returns true for the errors dataset with no query check, and the endpoint then sends yAxis/selected_columns of "upsampled_count() as count" to that dataset. Unless the errors dataset shares this exact converter, allowlisted errors-dataset stats queries will fail function resolution instead of returning an upsampled count. The integration tests only hit discover via event.type:error and do not cover dataset=errors.

Accidental gitlink pins a nested copy of the repository

This change adds a gitlink/submodule named sentry-repo whose commit is the PR base (a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a). It is unrelated to error upsampling. Checking out the branch will try to materialize a nested repository (or fail if the gitlink has no .gitmodules URL), and it should not be merged.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache pins false denies and skips permission refresh

Check writes a 30s denial (userPermDenialCacheKey) whenever the DB-backed check returns false, and the next Check returns that denial before consulting either the permission cache or the database. A negative result is often stale rather than authoritative: checkInheritedPermissions uses the separately cached folder tree, so a dashboard/folder under a newly created parent is denied even when the user has folders:uid:<parent> (or a permission row that was committed after the check). That false deny is then sticky for shortCacheTTL, including after the folder cache expires and after a later grant, which re-breaks the create-then-access case this PR is fixing. Denial entries are never deleted on a successful refresh.

Cached check error skips the DB permission fallback

If getCachedIdentityPermissions hits but checkPermission fails (typically buildFolderTree / folder store error while evaluating inheritance), Check returns the error immediately. It never reaches getIdentityPermissions, so a direct scope that exists only in the DB (the newly created dashboard/folder permission this change is meant to observe) is never loaded. A transient folder-store failure therefore fails the request even when the refreshed permission set would allow without walking the folder tree.

Warm permission cache no longer serves distinct denies

A permission-cache hit that does not contain the requested scope is treated as a miss and always calls getIdentityPermissions, which no longer reads the cache and always queries the DB (and then overwrites permCache). Previously one cached scope map answered every Check for that user and action. Now each distinct denied (namespace, user, action, name, folder) tuple hits the database until its denial entry is warm. Authorizing a page or search over many resources the user cannot access becomes a query stampede, and concurrent refreshes can also overwrite a newer permCache entry with an older snapshot.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

Login-cache invalidation uses wrapped isEnabled and skips real membership changes

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate treats the pre-update model from getById as the source of truth for whether the IdP is a login IdP. With the organization feature on, getById returns a wrapper whose isEnabled() is false whenever the linked organization is missing, disabled, or the organization provider is disabled, even if the stored IdP is enabled. LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate uses that isEnabled(). The getForLogin cache, however, is filled from the JPA query, which only checks the IdP's own enabled, link-only, hide-on-login, and broker-public flags. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write path never rechecks cache and can wipe a good value

GetWebAssets drops the read lock, then later takes the write lock and always reloads and assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result (line 69), including when the load fails and result is nil. There is no second check of entryPointAssetsCache under the write lock. Two callers can both observe a nil cache; the first populates it successfully and the second then overwrites that pointer with nil (or a redundant load) if its file read fails. Later non-dev requests miss the cache and fail until a later load succeeds. After Lock(), return the existing cache when Env is not Dev and it is already non-nil, and do not store a nil/error result over a successful one.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate points out the same missing re-check of the cache after the write lock is taken. This is the incomplete double-checked locking that the golden comment describes. The candidate also adds a related consequence about a failed load overwriting a good value, which does not change the core match.
